title: Core Concepts
summary: Why wunder behaves the way it does—9 core design constraints, along with the layers they form, the entries into them, and the reading paths.
text: Core Concepts Why wunder behaves the way it does—9 core design constraints, along with the layers they form, the entries into them, and the reading paths. wunder is an agent-scheduling platform: hand it a goal and it breaks the task down, calls tools, and delivers results. These 9 cores explain why the system behaves the way it does, not a list of what it can do. For the feature list, see Tools and the API Index. Four design principles | Principle | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Everything revolves around the thread | The thread (= session) is the unit of execution, not "one Q&A". A single agent can hold several independent task threads at once, and scheduling, locks, and realtime state are all isolated per thread | | Everything is a tool | Everything the model can do is exposed through a unified tool interface; canonical names are mostly Chinese (读取文件, 执行命令, 记忆管理), and English aliases are normalized before routing | | One engine across forms | There is only one core and one engine; the four forms differ only at the access layer | | Boundaries and governance are built in | Prompt freezing, approval tiers, daily quotas, and bounded views with pagination are part of the skeleton, not left to the upper layers | The four forms | Form | Role | | --- | --- | | Honeycomb (desktop) | A local AI workbench, the default entry for individuals; a local desktop process that calls the engine in-process, with a local SQLite | | Beehive (web) | A cloud AI workbench reached from a browser; no process of its own, using the Hull's storage | | Helm (cli) | A hands-on local entry driven from a terminal and easy to script; a local process with a local SQLite | | Hull (server) | The user- and agent-management platform: multi-tenancy, units, app build-and-release, and gateway access; a service process plus the engine, with the Bridge built in | The Honeycomb and the Helm do not depend on the Hull and can run and ship on their own. The Electron / Tauri front-end shells are no longer maintained day to day and are no longer described as a capability. The 9 cores Goal Lets an agent enter goal mode and keep working on one task. Compatibility Lets the Honeycomb and the Helm run in older operating-system environments under explicit constraints. Context compression Keeps context size under control in long conversations while retaining useful information. Subagents Forks a subtask inside a single thread; an independent executor completes it and returns the result. Scheduled tasks Supports system-level periodic execution and background governance. Channels Connects multiple entries to the same runtime capability. Memory Supports long conversations and long-term material use without polluting the thread's core cognition. Multi-threading Raises throughput and resource use through concurrency control inside a single process. Multi-tenancy Supports the Hull's organization, user, tenant, and permission governance. The layers, from the inside out: | Layer | Cores | What they solve | | --- | --- | --- | | Execution engine | context compression, memory, subagents, multi-threading | How one thread runs to completion: it can control its length, use long-term material, fork subtasks, and advance concurrently with other threads | | Access and governance | channels, scheduled tasks, multi-tenancy, goal | Who wakes a thread and when, plus the governance surface of organizations, users, and permissions | | Platform foundation | compatibility | Which operating systems this engine and its access layer can run on | Going deeper by topic One layer down, by topic (all under Reference › In Depth): | Topic | Page | | --- | --- | | Which stages a message passes through | Architecture | | How sessions, threads, and rounds are numbered | Sessions and Rounds | | Realtime push and resuming after a disconnect | Streaming Execution | | Workspaces and file safety | Workspaces and Working Directory | | Status indicators | Runtime State | | Tool sources and governance | Tool System | | The four layers of prompts, skills, and capabilities | Prompts and Skills | | Memory shapes and troubleshooting | Long-term Memory | | Tokens and quotas | Tokens and Quotas | | Persistent goal mode | Goal Mode | | Animated companions | Companion System | | Anomaly and truncation behavior | Boundary Handling | | How a thread advances round by round | Agent Loop | | The four layers of capabilities | Tools | | The process is visible and a disconnect can resume | Realtime | | Bounded views, budgets, and circuit breaking | Stability | | Logs, metrics, and thread trajectories | Observability | Recommended reading by role First time on the Honeycomb: Quickstart → Agent Loop → Tools → Memory → Context Compression. Administrator / governance: Multi-user Management → Stability → Observability → Channels → Configuration Reference. Integration and development: Architecture → Chat WebSocket → Streaming Execution. Common misconceptions "Several agents can form a swarm and collaborate" — they cannot. The only collaborative form is the subagent: a temporary work unit the main agent creates and reclaims when the task ends. Swarm orchestration (swarm tools, hives, orchestration mode, team runs, swarm packs) has been removed from the engine and the scheduling surface; a few terminal strings and UI labels still carry the old wording, but that is leftover to clean up, not a capability. "Every listed tool is usable" — it is not. The default usable set is a fixed tier, and 网页搜索 and ptc are currently temporarily withdrawn (code kept, invisible to model and user), not deleted. "Editing the prompt affects the current conversation at once" — it does not. Once a thread first fixes its system prompt, it is frozen. "What the UI shows is the back-end truth" — the UI consumes a bounded view (pagination plus a byte budget), not the full history. When the content looks wrong, trust the thread ledger. "Stopping maintenance of the front-end shell stops the Honeycomb back end" — they are two different things. The Honeycomb runs the local native UI with in-process native calls by default, and its execution, tools, and storage semantics still reuse the engine. Further reading Architecture — stages and links Sessions and Rounds — counting conventions Glossary — consistent wording Four design principles The four forms The 9 cores Going deeper by topic Recommended reading by role Common misconceptions Further reading

title: Goal
summary: The Goal core lets an agent enter goal mode and keep working on one task: three tools drive it, four phases, a default 256-round cap, and automatic blocking after 3 consecutive rounds without progress.
text: Goal The Goal core lets an agent enter goal mode and keep working on one task: three tools drive it, four phases, a default 256-round cap, and automatic blocking after 3 consecutive rounds without progress. # Goal The Goal core lets an agent enter goal mode and keep working on one task. Attach a goal to a session and the agent carries on by itself, until it completes, is blocked, or exhausts the round budget. How it works A goal is driven by three tools: | Tool | Role | | --- | --- | | getgoal | Reads the current goal and its revision | | creategoal | Creates a goal | | updategoal | Edits, pauses, resumes, completes, or reports blocked | A goal has only four phases: active, paused, blocked, complete. Updates use CAS-on-revision: an update must carry the goal's current revision, and a mismatch is rejected. Started rounds only ever increase. Key numbers | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Default goal round cap | 256 | | Automatic blocking after no progress | 3 rounds | | Phase values | active / paused / blocked / complete | Where it is used | Entry | Location | | --- | --- | | Interface | /wunder/chat/sessions/{id}/goal | | Slash command | /goal | Boundaries and current limits There is no token budget and no cooldown between rounds. Whether a goal stops depends on three things only: the round budget, the phase, and whether it is armed. The armed state is not persisted: after a process restart or a session resume, even if the phase is still active, an explicit updategoal action=resume is needed to arm it again. When asking "why has the goal stopped moving", check first whether it is armed. The desktop form does not expose goal selection; the runtime injects it per session. The Bridge has no goal UI; goal operations happen in the Beehive, the Honeycomb, and the Helm. Goal How it works Key numbers Where it is used Boundaries and current limits

title: Compatibility
summary: The Compatibility core lets the Honeycomb (desktop) and the Helm (cli) run in older operating-system environments under explicit constraints: Windows 7 32-bit and Ubuntu 18.04 each have an offline build chain, and the interface uses software rendering that does not depend on a GPU.
text: Compatibility The Compatibility core lets the Honeycomb (desktop) and the Helm (cli) run in older operating-system environments under explicit constraints: Windows 7 32-bit and Ubuntu 18.04 each have an offline build chain, and the interface uses software rendering that does not depend on a GPU. # Compatibility The Compatibility core lets the Honeycomb (desktop) and the Helm (cli) run in older operating-system environments, and states explicitly where that runtime environment is constrained. Which older systems are supported | System | Approach | | --- | --- | | Windows 7, 32-bit | A dedicated i686-win7-windows-gnu Tier 3 target plus a build-std offline toolchain | | Ubuntu 18.04 x64 / arm64 | An offline build chain and sysroot | Why it runs The interface does not depend on a GPU: Slint uses software rendering. Building does not depend on network access: both the Windows 7 32-bit and the Ubuntu 18.04 chains are offline toolchains, and the Ubuntu side carries a sysroot as well. Command sessions adapt to old terminals: command sessions are carried over winpty, and output is decoded as GBK. Startup recovery scan and self-check: recovery scanning and self-checking run at startup. What it means for users Windows 7 32-bit and Ubuntu 18.04 (x64 / arm64) are not excluded runtime environments; the Honeycomb and the Helm can be installed on old machines and run there. The interface renders on machines without a GPU. Command sessions are carried and decoded in old Windows terminals. Boundaries and current limits Build scripts still carry dead Tauri links — pointing at directories that no longer exist. That is an engineering gap and says nothing about capability. win7 interlink nodes do not declare tool.exec, so the capability surface of old devices is narrower. Compatibility Which older systems are supported Why it runs What it means for users Boundaries and current limits

title: Context Compression
summary: Long conversations are not cut short when they grow long. The system trims history in graded levels, keeps the most useful information, and lets the conversation continue.
headings: What it protects and what it leaves alone
text: Context Compression Long conversations are not cut short when they grow long. The system trims history in graded levels, keeps the most useful information, and lets the conversation continue. ## Why compression is needed An agent's "memory" has a ceiling — the history a single conversation can carry cannot grow without bound, and the model's context window sets that limit. As a conversation grows longer, the total of history plus tool results can exceed the ceiling. Context compression trims the history without interrupting the conversation, keeping the most useful information so the conversation keeps running. Compression is not deletion. Deletion cuts content outright, regardless of importance; compression reorganizes content, keeping the key facts and trimming the redundant parts. How compression is graded Compression escalates from gentle to aggressive only when necessary: | Level | Strategy | Degree of loss | | --- | --- | --- | | Level 1 | Remove intermediate tool results | Very low; tool results can be fetched again | | Level 2 | Summarize historical messages | Medium; keeps semantics, loses detail | | Level 3 | Remove earlier conversation rounds | Higher; keeps only the most recent content | | Level 4 | Keep only the core setup and the current request | Very high; emergency degradation | What it protects and what it leaves alone Without compression, a long conversation ends in one of three ways: an outright error, a brute-force truncation, or manual control of conversation length. Compression is a system capability, so conversation length needs no manual management. Compression protects three things first: the continuity of the conversation, so it is not interrupted for being too long; the facts genuinely needed, favoring information useful to the current task; and traceability, so every compression leaves a record of what it compressed and what it kept for administrators to inspect. There are two bottom lines. First, compression can only trim and reorganize existing content; it never invents. Second, a thread's core setup (the system prompt) is frozen at creation, and compression acts only on the conversation history and tool results, so an agent never "forgets who it is" because of compression. Compression is inspectable Every compression leaves a record that includes the strategy used, the context size before and after, and a rough assessment of the information lost. Administrators use it to judge whether compression has affected task quality. In practice These situations tend to trigger compression: a very long conversation (dozens of rounds or more), a tool returning a large amount of content (reading a large file, many search results), and complex multi-step tasks. To trigger it less often, open a new thread once a topic is done rather than keeping an old thread alive, keep prompts concise, and avoid pasting large repeated blocks; the /compact command triggers compression deliberately. After compression, quality mostly does not drop noticeably, because the system favors what the current task needs. Only in extreme cases (a very long conversation stacked with a large amount of tool output) might you notice the agent recalling early details less precisely, and then a new conversation thread is the fix. Local reduction comes first When automatic compression triggers, the system first sees whether earlier file reads, searches, and listing results can be shortened. The last 5 groups of tool results, error information, media, and results that still need pagination are protected. A shortened old result still carries its location, a head/tail preview, and an explicit omission notice, so the agent can read it again when needed. If the local reduction has already freed enough space, no extra model call is made to produce a summary; if not, the summary flow runs. Manual compression and overflow recovery go straight to summarization. A summary outputs at most 2048 tokens by default, and if the model itself is configured with a smaller output limit, the smaller one wins. Administrators can see the estimated savings of the local reduction in the progress records. The estimate is for diagnosis only; actual token consumption follows the model provider's report. Related pages Boundary Handling — system behavior under various boundary conditions Tokens and Quota — how context usage is measured Memory — the relationship between long-term data and context compression Why compression is needed How compression is graded What it protects and what it leaves alone Compression is inspectable In practice Local reduction comes first Related pages

title: Subagents
summary: The Subagents core forks a subtask inside a single thread for an independent executor to complete and return to the parent; the only collaborative form is the subagent, and swarm orchestration has been removed from the engine and the protocol layer.
text: Subagents The Subagents core forks a subtask inside a single thread for an independent executor to complete and return to the parent; the only collaborative form is the subagent, and swarm orchestration has been removed from the engine and the protocol layer. # Subagents The Subagents core forks a subtask inside a single thread: the parent thread hands one subtask to an independent executor, which runs it and passes the result back to the parent thread. How it works 子智能体控制 (Subagent Control) provides 11 actions: | Action | Action | Action | | --- | --- | --- | | spawn | batchspawn | wait | | interrupt | close | resume | | report | send | status | | list | history | | Parent–child round references are encoded as userround + modelround, and an executor's rounds hang under that pair of parent round references. The sub-session's user message is hidden, and it wakes with auto-wake. Boundaries and current limits The only collaborative form is the subagent. Swarm orchestration (swarm tools, hives, orchestration mode, team runs, swarm packs) has been removed from the engine and the protocol layer; it is not waiting to be implemented, nor hidden behind a switch. Swarm leftovers remain in TUI prompts, front-end i18n labels, and compatibility shims, and empty directories await cleanup. Those leftovers do not mean the capability exists. Subagents How it works Boundaries and current limits

title: Scheduled Tasks
summary: Scheduled tasks run the agent at a chosen time: three schedule kinds — at for a one-off point, every for a fixed interval, cron for a recurring pattern — with leases, backoff, and auto-disable, so tasks survive a process restart.
headings: Where to create one, and support by form
text: Scheduled Tasks Scheduled tasks run the agent at a chosen time: three schedule kinds — at for a one-off point, every for a fixed interval, cron for a recurring pattern — with leases, backoff, and auto-disable, so tasks survive a process restart. Scheduled tasks let the agent run automatically at a chosen time, for periodic reports, inspections, and reminders. This is engine-level scheduling: the task definition is persisted in storage, and a background loop claims work by due time, independent of which session you happen to be viewing. Every run is recorded (/wunder/cron/runs): whether it ran, whether it succeeded, and when it will run next; failures come with backoff and auto-disable; and a process restart does not lose the task definitions. This differs from waiting inside a session: yielding in a session only affects the current thread, whereas a scheduled task creates a new run in the future. Scheduled tasks diagram: scheduling rules enter the scheduler, then dispatch to background execution and execution records Three kinds of schedule The kind field is one of at, every, or cron. | Kind | Semantics | Input | Bounds | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | at | One-off point in time | An RFC3339 timestamp | At most 365 days ahead; auto-disabled once it runs (disabled with a reason if it fails) | | every | Fixed interval | everyms (optional start time) | 1,000 ms ≤ interval ≤ 86,400,000 ms (24 hours) | | cron | Recurring expression | A 5–7 field expression plus an optional timezone | Fields accept only digits and / - , ?; the timezone is parsed as a named timezone, defaulting to the local timezone | Natural language also works in tools and quick input, and the system converts it into the kinds above: every 5 minutes becomes a fixed interval, and daily at 9am and weekdays at 6pm become the corresponding cron expressions; when it cannot parse the input, it suggests the formats that are accepted. Content limits: a task name is at most 128 characters, and a trigger message at most 16,384 characters. Where results are delivered sessiontarget has two values. | Value | Behavior | | --- | --- | | main (default) | The result is delivered to the bound current session, continuing the same conversation | | isolated | Each run creates a separate thread session and keeps a link back to the parent session | Choose isolated for recurring tasks that need a trail and should not disturb the main conversation; choose main when you want the result appended directly to the existing context. Execution guarantees In multi-instance deployments a lease prevents duplicate execution: when a task is claimed, the runner's identity, a run token, and a lease expiry are written, and the lease is renewed with a heartbeat while the run lasts; if the process crashes, the lease expires and another instance can claim the task. Each record also carries a deduplication key and a consecutive-failure count, and writes down why it was disabled. Default scheduling parameters: | Parameter | Default | | --- | --- | | Max concurrent runs | 1 | | Poll interval | 1000 ms | | Max idle sleep | 5000 ms | | Lease lifetime / heartbeat | 300 seconds / 60 seconds | | Consecutive-failure auto-disable threshold | 5 | After a failure, backoff steps up with the consecutive-failure count: 30 seconds → 60 seconds → 5 minutes → 15 minutes → 1 hour, then stays at the last step. Once the failure limit is reached, the task is auto-disabled with a written reason; re-enabling it resets the failure count. The master switch With the master switch off (cron.enabled=false), only four kinds of write operation are rejected — add, update, enable, and run (each with a clear message). Status, list, a single detail, run records, delete, and disable all remain available, so existing tasks can still be reviewed and cleaned up. This is not a blanket refusal of the whole interface. Where to create one, and support by form | Surface | Status | | --- | --- | | API | /wunder/cron/, 11 endpoints in all (status / list / runs / add / update / remove / enable / disable / get / run / action), on the user side, isolated by user ownership | | Tool | The built-in scheduled-tasks tool (canonical name 定时任务, alias scheduletask), sharing the same handler as the API, so the model can create tasks on its own | | Beehive | A scheduled-tasks category page under settings | | Honeycomb | A scheduled-tasks page plus a native entry point, calling the same handler in-process | | Helm | No scheduled tasks: the local engine explicitly disables the scheduler at startup, and there is no related slash command | | Bridge | No user-level task management page; it exists only as a template configuration under preset agents | When you need something to run on a schedule, configure it on the Beehive, the Honeycomb, or the Hull side. Related pages Schedule Task — tool parameters and usage Stability — the wider view of backoff and bounded design Agent Loop — how a triggered task enters the execution chain Three kinds of schedule Where results are delivered Execution guarantees The master switch Where to create one, and support by form Related pages

title: Channels
summary: Feishu, QQ, WeChat, XMPP, and generic webhooks differ in support level; an inbound message is routed to its agent and workspace by binding.
headings: A channel is only an entry point
How a message finds its agent and workspace
The boundaries of inbound, outbound, and rate limiting
text: Channels Feishu, QQ, WeChat, XMPP, and generic webhooks differ in support level; an inbound message is routed to its agent and workspace by binding. ## A channel is only an entry point All execution happens in the engine. A channel does just two things: parse an external message into a unified inbound shape, and deliver the unified outbound shape back into an external protocol. Protocol adaptation stops at the entry; a channel does not copy business logic, does not keep its own storage, and does not change thread semantics. So the same task thread can take a message from Beehive, continue it from Feishu, and finish it from Honeycomb; a channel never creates a second execution path. A form (Honeycomb / Beehive / Helm / Hull) is the shape of running and access; a channel (Feishu / QQ / WeChat …) is an off-site platform. Which channels are supported today Feishu (feishu): a persistent connection plus a webhook, fully implemented, with a dedicated webhook entry point. QQ Bot (qqbot): a persistent connection plus a webhook, fully implemented, with a dedicated webhook entry point. WeChat (weixin): runs on a persistent connection (iLink long polling), fully implemented, and the largest in scale. XMPP (xmpp): a persistent connection plus a webhook. It is disabled by default and is only a placeholder then, returning a "not enabled" notice for all send and receive; it becomes a real implementation only once explicitly turned on. WeCom (wechat): webhook only, partially implemented (send, receive, and signature verification), with no persistent connection. WeChat Official Account (wechatmp): webhook only, partially implemented, with no persistent connection. WhatsApp Cloud (whatsappcloud): webhook only, partially implemented, with no persistent connection. Only four channels use a persistent connection: Feishu, QQ Bot, XMPP, and WeChat (weixin). WeCom, the Official Account, and WhatsApp Cloud are pure webhook callbacks. The following platforms have no adapter at all: telegram, discord, slack, LINE, DingTalk. They exist only as generic-webhook directory entries, handled through the generic entry point and generic parsing — with no platform-specific signature verification, rich-text mapping, attachment download, or proactive push. The accurate statement is that they are visible in the directory and can send and receive text over a generic webhook, but they have no platform-specific adapter. How a message finds its agent and workspace An inbound message is first resolved by binding: candidates are scored by specificity, the single best one is taken, and priority breaks a tie. | Dimension | Score | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | Exact peerid match | 8 | Supports the wildcard, and a wildcard scores nothing | | peerkind match | 4 | dm/direct/single/user are treated as the same kind | | accountid match | 2 | Empty means wildcard | | channel match | 1 | Empty means wildcard | A hit yields the target agent and any tool overrides, after which the workspace is decided: empty, as well as the default and default aliases, all point to that user's default agent workspace. In the Hull form, workspaces are flattened per user into a single cloud directory, so files arriving from different channels for the same user land in the same place. The boundaries of inbound, outbound, and rate limiting Inbound uses a bounded queue: capacity 512, concurrency 8, enqueue timeout 80 ms. A full queue or an enqueue timeout counts as backpressure and reports "queue busy" rather than piling up without limit. The visible effect is that the platform redelivers or briefly delays; messages are not silently dropped. Outbound runs on a persistent queue with exponential backoff, defaulting to a 500 ms polling interval, batches of 50, and at most 5 retries, with a backoff base of 2 s and a ceiling of 60 s. Outbound delivery has a switch. When it is off, delivery is instead attempted once synchronously at enqueue time and is no longer redelivered by the polling loop. When troubleshooting a "received but no reply" case, check this switch first: once it is off and that one synchronous attempt fails, the message sits in the outbound queue waiting for manual handling. Rate limiting is a token bucket of QPS plus a concurrency cap per channel account; both at 0 means no limiting. A rate-limited request does not consume a concurrency slot and is handed to the outbound queue for backoff redelivery. Attachments and media Inbound media is downloaded, transcoded, and dropped into the workspace for that channel before being handed to the engine; platform-specific files have their own download entry points and likewise write into the workspace; and a further kind of pending file is reserved first and fetched on demand. Outbound attachments are extracted from the body, from Markdown, or from a workspace path and then uploaded. Channel clients usually do not understand internal paths, so attachments go out as an upload link rather than a path string thrown at the user. Webhook entry points and verification The generic entry point is POST /wunder/channel/{provider}/webhook; Feishu and QQ Bot have their own dedicated entry points at POST /wunder/channel/feishu/webhook and POST /wunder/channel/qqbot/webhook. Verification differs by platform: some loop back a verification token from configuration, some use a content signature, and WeCom additionally verifies the signature and decrypts the encrypted message. The generic webhook does no platform-specific verification, so platforms that use the generic entry point need to close this off themselves at a gateway or reverse proxy to guarantee a trustworthy source. Troubleshooting message problems 1. Presence: for a persistent-connection channel, check whether its connection process is running; a webhook-only channel has no notion of presence, so check only whether the callback arrives. 2. Whether the callback arrives: check the platform-side push logs and the channel's runtime logs. 3. Whether it was routed: check the binding score and the enabled state; a binding to a different agent looks exactly like no response at all. 4. Arrived but no reply: check for records stuck in the outbound queue, whether the outbound delivery loop is off, and whether rate limiting was hit. 5. XMPP specifics: confirm whether it is enabled — while disabled by default it is only a placeholder, and errors say so directly. Points not to mix up telegram / discord / slack / LINE / DingTalk have no adapter; they are only generic directory entries. WeCom and the Official Account have no persistent connection; only Feishu, QQ Bot, XMPP, and WeChat have one. XMPP is not usable out of the box; while disabled by default it is a placeholder. A channel cannot be configured with business logic; it has only two layers, the target agent and tool overrides, and everything else lives in the engine and on the management side. The core capabilities are the same across channels; the differences are only in protocol expression (rich text, attachments, cards) and whether a persistent connection is supported. The inbound queue does not guarantee no loss by queuing forever; it is bounded at 512 with an 80 ms enqueue timeout, and anything beyond goes to backpressure and platform redelivery. A failed outbound delivery is not dropped outright; it uses a persistent queue with exponential backoff and at most 5 retries. Honeycomb and Helm do not go through the channel layer: Honeycomb is a native in-process call, and Helm uses its own access path. title: Memory
summary: Long-term data is injected once when a thread is created and stays frozen afterwards; it has two layers, initialization injection and runtime recall.
headings: A few rules that go with it
text: Memory Long-term data is injected once when a thread is created and stays frozen afterwards; it has two layers, initialization injection and runtime recall. ## What problem memory solves An agent needs to "remember" long-term information — who the user is, what they prefer, what policies an organization has, what background a project has. If such material is cobbled together on the fly every time, the agent's behavior swings between good and bad. wunder's approach is to inject it once when the thread is created and keep it frozen afterwards, never rewriting it dynamically on every round. Three things follow: cognitive boundaries stay stable while the thread runs, so it does not drift as the conversation goes on; the system prompt stays stable, which helps cache acceleration; and it can clearly answer what background this thread started from. The two layers of memory The first layer is thread-initialization injection. When a thread is created, the system writes the key long-term material into the system prompt, where it becomes the thread's cognitive base. The second layer is runtime supplementary retrieval. If more material is needed during execution, the system retrieves it dynamically through recall rather than rewriting the system prompt. Who it helps For ordinary users: personal preferences are remembered and take effect automatically in new conversations; the agent does not "forget" who the user is as a conversation goes on; and the agent can use long-term material in the workspace and knowledge base. For administrators: memory-injection rules are controllable, which keeps sensitive information from leaking; conversations of the same kind start from the same background, so results are more predictable; and a thread's initialization background can be traced. What memory looks like Memory uses structured fragments rather than one long free-text block. Fragments are found by lookup, replaced individually without affecting the rest, marked invalid when outdated, and carry traceable version relationships. A few rules that go with it Once the system prompt is set it stays frozen, and later conversation never modifies it dynamically, which keeps thread behavior stable. Long-term memory is injected only once at thread creation; even if recall fires during a run, its result is only supplementary reference and never rewrites the system prompt. Workspaces, knowledge bases, and memory can all supply material, but their responsibilities differ: | Source | Character | Use | | --- | --- | --- | | Workspace | The scene of the current task | Holds the files being worked on | | Knowledge base | A long-term document source | Retrieves policies, material, and reference documents | | Memory | Structured accumulation | Remembers who the user is, their preferences, and past decisions | In practice When a memory update takes effect depends on the thread: a newly created thread applies the latest memory automatically, while an existing thread is unaffected and keeps the copy from when it was created. So after you update a personal preference, a new conversation is needed for it to take effect. Memory and context compression have different jobs: compression governs near-field information such as conversation history, while memory supplies far-field information such as long-term background. Compression does not touch the memory inside the system prompt. More memory is not better. Injecting too much crowds the conversation's context space, introduces irrelevant information that disturbs judgment, and raises token consumption. The system therefore has intelligent selection and limiting mechanisms and does not inject without bound. A few clarifications Memory does not update automatically every round; it is injected only at initialization and does not change during a run. Recall is a dynamic supplement and does not rewrite the base. Workspace files are not the same as memory either — a workspace is the scene of the current task, while memory is long-term accumulation. title: Multi-threading
summary: The Multi-threading core raises throughput and resource use through concurrency control inside a single process: one user can hold several concurrent task threads, backed by a session queue, session locks, a parallelism cap, and a daily quota.
text: Multi-threading The Multi-threading core raises throughput and resource use through concurrency control inside a single process: one user can hold several concurrent task threads, backed by a session queue, session locks, a parallelism cap, and a daily quota. # Multi-threading The Multi-threading core raises throughput and resource use through concurrency control inside a single process: a single user can hold several task threads at once, and scheduling, locks, and realtime state are isolated per thread. How it works The engine-level session queue is enabled by default, with 会话让出 as the way to yield. A session lock has a TTL of 120 seconds with heartbeat renewal; when its holder exits abnormally, the TTL releases it. Tool parallelism ≤ 4: tools that run in parallel take a read lock, and tools that run exclusively take a write lock. Round caps, active-session caps, daily quotas, and retry circuit breaking form four hard constraints. Key numbers | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Session lock TTL | 120 seconds (with heartbeat) | | Tool parallelism | ≤ 4 | | Round cap | 1000 by default | Boundaries and current limits With agentqueue.enabled turned off, sending another message while a run is in progress is judged "user busy" and no longer enters the queue bar (the Hull warns about this at startup). This is a configuration choice, not a fault. Blocking category quotas and bounded queues are hard caps: when full, the system reports busy and does not wait in a queue.
