title: Beehive Interface
summary: The Beehive is the cloud AI workbench, provided with the Hull deployment and reached in a browser. Its settings include tools, memory, channels, scheduled tasks, devices, and archive; it supports two-way voice (TTS included) and has no interactive terminal.
text: Beehive Interface The Beehive is the cloud AI workbench, provided with the Hull deployment and reached in a browser. Its settings include tools, memory, channels, scheduled tasks, devices, and archive; it supports two-way voice (TTS included) and has no interactive terminal. # Beehive Interface The Beehive is wunder's cloud AI workbench: once the Hull is deployed, members open it in a browser and start working. It has no process of its own; the pages ship alongside the Hull deployment. Concretely, the built pages in frontend/dist are served by an nginx container (port 18001 by default) — the Hull itself only serves the Bridge's static directory, not the Beehive. Opening and signing in Open the deployed address in a browser. If you are not signed in you land on the login page, where you can register directly. After signing in you go straight to your agent's chat page. Chat: the main workspace, covered under "Main area" Embedded chat: a conversation embedded inside another page External workflow landing pages: pages for external flows reached by link Settings: you stay on the chat page, with the right side switching to the matching settings category Thread trajectory: the execution record of a whole thread Admin console: admins get separate user, agent, and system management pages after signing in Main area The Beehive's main area is a three-column chat workspace: Left column: new task, search, workspace and thread tree, working directory, settings entry Right column: chat top bar + timeline + input area Overlays: file preview, inline editing, companion overlay One agent can hold several independent task threads at once, and there can be several workspaces: your own cloud workspace (/workspaces/ /workspace) plus remote device workspaces reached through device interconnection. Realtime updates and connectivity All realtime traffic runs over a single WebSocket (/chat/ws), which the client multiplexes: new messages, execution progress, and approval prompts all arrive through it. The Beehive does not open several WebSocket channels at once. After a reconnect, the state is filled in by ordinary requests, so you do not have to reload the page. If the network or a proxy blocks that one connection, realtime state stops updating; refreshing the page usually restores it. Rendering long conversations The timeline does not lay out an entire thread at once; it loads by window as you scroll, so a long thread does not freeze when opened. Parsing and rendering also run in background workers, so they do not block the main thread. The rendering optimization for extremely large threads is a rewritten plan whose production implementation is not fully in place. Very long threads can still stutter. Settings categories The Beehive's settings hang off the chat page as categories and share the same backend capabilities as the Honeycomb. They include: General / Account / Models / Agent / Companion / Prompt packs / Help (the same as the Honeycomb) Tools: four tabs — built-in / MCP / skills / knowledge bases Memory: long-term memory management Channels: channel binding and status Scheduled: scheduled tasks Devices: entry to device-interconnection management Archive: archived threads Differences from the Honeycomb | Item | Beehive | Honeycomb | | --- | --- | --- | | Running mode | Reached in a browser, in the cloud | A desktop app installed on your own computer | | Data storage | Hull storage | Local | | Interactive terminal | ❌ No | ✅ Yes | | Voice input / output | Both directions ✅ (TTS included) | Input ✅, output ❌ | | Device interconnection | ✅ Devices category + interconnection view | ⚠️ Cloud workspace + approval pop-up only; settings category not opened | | Tray / system notifications / global hotkey / screenshot | ❌ | ✅ | | Attachment upload limit | Temporary attachments 200 MB, persistent attachments 10 MB | Local files referenced directly | Input area Message input: natural language, plus slash commands Attachments: pick locally or drag and drop Send / stop: sends when idle, turns into stop while running Model switch: change models right in the input area, without jumping to settings Approval mode: Suggest / Auto-edit / Fully automatic (fully automatic by default) Reasoning level: the brain icon at the bottom; gray follows the model, while empty / half-full / full mean no thinking / medium / highest Work-thread panel: shares the same outer panel as the working directory; a status icon and activity count stay at the right of the title; the filter button remains after all activity ends, so you can leave the filter at any time, and drag-to-reorder still works while filtering Timeline and status Below each reply, "Work process" folds away intermediate thinking, tool batches, and interim output Status: 🔄 Running / ⏳ Waiting (needs your input or approval) / ✅ Complete Context usage and duration belong to the model request that issued the tool; tools running in parallel within one request share the same numbers and are not added up per entry Very fast calls may show 0ms; failed and cancelled calls also record their duration Slash commands Type them into the message box: /new — create a new thread /stop — stop the current execution /compact — compress the conversation on demand /help — open the help docs /goal — goal management /compact also counts as one user turn; the compressed summary appears right in the reply bubble after the command and survives switching threads or refreshing the page. Protection mechanisms Attachment processing: the send button is disabled until processing finishes Background running: switching, creating, refreshing, or briefly going offline does not cancel running work threads; once you reconnect, status and pending approvals are restored from saved events Empty-thread reuse: a new thread prefers an empty thread the current agent has not used yet; threads that have sent messages, are running, or were spawned by subagents are never reused Deletion sync: after an admin deletes a thread, your side clears the entry and its cache on the next list refresh or switch; clicking a stale entry shows a notice and returns you to the input page Common questions The Beehive and the Bridge are two separate interfaces: the Beehive faces users, the Bridge faces admins, and the two are kept apart. The Beehive is built for sharing: it is itself a team / multi-user setting, where members sign in with a Hull account. For a single machine, the Honeycomb is recommended. The Beehive has no terminal: when you need a shell, use the Honeycomb or the Helm. Voice output (TTS) works here: the Beehive supports two-way voice, TTS included; the Honeycomb is input-only, with no playback. How device interconnection is used: the Beehive is the full entry; settings live under the "Devices" category, and command approvals pop up inline in the timeline. Further Reading Interface Overview Honeycomb Interface Bridge Interface Hull deployment Troubleshooting Beehive Interface Opening and signing in Main area Realtime updates and connectivity Rendering long conversations Settings categories Differences from the Honeycomb Input area Timeline and status Slash commands Protection mechanisms Common questions Further Reading

title: Bridge Interface
summary: The Bridge is the Hull's governance and debugging console. Its top-level navigation has 4 groups and 19 items: System 4, Agents 6, Debug 6, Docs 2.
headings: What the Bridge does not have
text: Bridge Interface The Bridge is the Hull's governance and debugging console. Its top-level navigation has 4 groups and 19 items: System 4, Agents 6, Debug 6, Docs 2. # Bridge Interface The Bridge is the governance and debugging console built into the Hull (the user and agent management platform). Regular users never see it after signing in; only administrators get in. It starts along with the Hull, with no separate build step, and shares the Hull's port (18000 by default). The Beehive and it are two separate interfaces: the Beehive faces users, the Bridge faces admins. Top-level navigation The Bridge has 4 groups and 19 items. System (4) Internal status: process health, locks and queues, runtime metrics System settings: hot-update configuration while running Organization management: the organization tree, up to 4 levels deep User management: accounts, quotas, and online status (split by Beehive / Honeycomb / Helm) Agents (6) Model configuration: LLM / TTS / image / video models Thread management: a cross-user thread list with status and goal state (read-only display, with no goal editor) Preset agents: agent templates that can declare which fields users may customize; user-level scheduled tasks and channels exist here as templates rather than as separate navigation items Companion management Tool management: groups built-in tools, MCP, knowledge bases, skills, and tool visibility together System prompts: prompt templates Debug (6) Throughput test: preset inputs from 1024 bytes to 1 MiB and outputs from 1024 to 8192, with a maximum concurrency of 1024 Performance test: uses fixed test users and a separate data root, with a 5-second command timeout Capability evaluation: runs capability benchmarks and scores them Multimodal debugging: direct tests of image / video / transcription / speech synthesis Debug panel: thread list + thread details; the log area on the right is now a thread-trajectory view LSP: language service Docs (2) Manual: the whole manual embedded in the console API: the API documentation entry What the Bridge does not have A user-level scheduled-task panel: there is no separate entry; scheduling exists only as a template under "Preset agents" User-level channel management: the same — channels live only in preset templates A long-term memory panel: not implemented An interconnection governance panel: fleet / channel / command / audit / policy governance for device interconnection is backend-API-only for now, with no interface; it is not true that the Bridge can govern interconnection Goal editing: thread management is read-only, with no goal editor; goal entry points are on the user side — the Beehive timeline, the Honeycomb input area, and the Helm's /goal command Usage notes Operations in the Bridge are high-risk by default: Key actions all have clear status, error feedback, and confirmation boundaries; a front-end confirmation does not replace backend permission checks Tables, logs, and monitoring panels use pagination / filtering / limits, so they never dump a large amount of data at once The interface is dense and made for scanning Access Address: http:// :18000/ (the default port, changeable in configuration) Authentication: admins sign in with an API key or login credentials; an organization head can manage only their own organization unit and its user accounts Change the default password right after the first sign-in Common questions The Bridge does not chat: it is the governance and debugging console; for daily conversation, use the Beehive or the Honeycomb. The Bridge and the Beehive are two separate interfaces: the Beehive is the user side and the Bridge is the admin side, kept apart. Why status shows interconnection and memory entries while the panels are empty: these are leftover dead entries; the panels were never implemented, and interconnection governance is backend-API-only for now. The log area is now a thread-trajectory view: the former log area on the right of the debug panel has been rebuilt as a thread-trajectory view, with the old log output kept only as a fallback. How the throughput test, the performance test, and the thread stress test differ: the throughput and performance tests are the Bridge's operations panels; the rendering-oriented thread stress test belongs to the user side, where the three interfaces default to 1000×1000. Further Reading Hull deployment Interface Overview Configuration reference Admin panels Bridge Interface Top-level navigation What the Bridge does not have Usage notes Access Common questions Further Reading

title: Honeycomb Interface
summary: The Honeycomb (desktop) is the local AI workbench and the default entry for individual users. Its main window has only two pages, chat and settings, with 12 categories in settings; everything else appears as panels and dialogs.
headings: The main window: only two pages
Capabilities that do not work yet
One-click reset of the working state
text: Honeycomb Interface The Honeycomb (desktop) is the local AI workbench and the default entry for individual users. Its main window has only two pages, chat and settings, with 12 categories in settings; everything else appears as panels and dialogs. # Honeycomb Interface The Honeycomb is wunder's local AI workbench, and the default entry for individual users. It runs entirely on your own computer: there is no separate backend port and no network relay, and the interface calls the local engine directly. Starting and running Open the desktop app: there is no port to specify and no required parameters. Data root: /.wunder; the WUNDERHOME environment variable moves it elsewhere Workspace: /.wunder/workspace Desktop settings: /config/desktop.settings.json A separate compatibility port (18123 by default) serves a few older clients only; day-to-day use never touches it The main window: only two pages The main window has two switchable pages, chat and settings; every other capability hangs off them as panels and dialogs. Chat page Two columns: Left column: tasks and thread tree, working directory, settings entry - The working directory shows both the local work tree and the cloud workspace - One agent can hold several independent task threads at once, and there can be several workspaces: the local directory, a cloud workspace, and remote device workspaces reached through device interconnection Right column: top bar (workspace / thread name) + timeline + input area - The welcome page shows when no thread is selected - The input area holds the model switch, approval mode, reasoning level, attachments, a voice-input button (when available), a screenshot button (when available), and send / stop - Below each reply, "Work process" folds away intermediate thinking, tool batches, and interim output Settings page 12 categories in all: | Category | Description | | --- | --- | | General | Interface language, appearance, startup behavior | | Account | Username, email, password, avatar | | Models | Add / edit LLM, TTS, image, and video models; TTS can be configured but not played | | Tools | Opens the tools dialog, grouped into built-in / MCP / skills / knowledge bases | | Agent | System prompt, default approval mode, default skill set | | Companion | Companion-package choice and floating-window size; the desktop floating window is Windows-only | | Scheduled | Entry to scheduled tasks | | Memory | Long-term memory management and hits | | Channels | Channel binding and status | | Prompt packs | Prompt packs available in-app, with language defaults | | Archive | Archived thread list | | Help | Embedded docs and version number | The category bar supports search filtering; when nothing matches it shows an empty state rather than a blank area. Panels and dialogs These are distinct areas inside the Honeycomb, not separate pages: Sidebar / timeline / input area: the three parts of the chat page Terminal view: an interactive command session where you type just as in a terminal Tools dialog: grouped into built-in / MCP / skills / knowledge bases Companion dialog: companion-package list and preview Workspace dialog: switch to or create a workspace Working directory: file tree + toolbar + usage bar + cloud workspace Thread trajectory: the execution ledger of a whole thread (it replaces the old log dialog) Subagent details Channels page: channel management on the user side Scheduled page: scheduled tasks on the user side Activity card / expert data / patch-diff card Screenshot overlay: a full-screen capture is pasted back into the input area Tray and system notifications: background running and completion reminders Remote command approval pop-up: a high-risk confirmation for interconnection commands, with a prominent border, risk level, and source details, plus a "cannot be remembered" prompt Capabilities unique to the Honeycomb These are not available in the other interfaces: | Capability | What it is | | --- | --- | | Interactive terminal | Run commands right inside it; the Beehive, the Bridge, and the Helm have none | | Screenshot capture | A full-screen capture pasted back into the input area | | Tray and system notifications | Reminders while running in the background and when a task finishes | | Global hotkey | Bring it up with a system-wide shortcut | | Voice input | Speak into the microphone and get text | | Local files and desktop control | Read and write local files and operate the desktop; needs vision capability | Capabilities that do not work yet The Device interconnection category in settings is not wired up: the entry exists in code but never renders, so it cannot be opened today. Interconnection in the Honeycomb lives in only two places — the cloud workspace under "Working directory" in the sidebar, and the remote-command approval pop-up. Voice output (TTS) is not implemented: TTS models can be configured in settings, but there is no playback; the voice side is input-only. For spoken output, use the Beehive. The early desktop shells are no longer maintained: the Electron / Tauri frontend shells receive no feature updates. This does not affect the Honeycomb's underlying engine. One-click reset of the working state When a session is stuck in the running state, a subagent's status is inconsistent, or the interface does not match reality, use Settings → General → Reset working state. It stops running sessions, clears queued tasks, and cleans up session locks and state. It keeps skills, knowledge bases, long-term memory, user configuration, workspace files, and session history. It cleans up the working state rather than performing a factory reset. Honeycomb vs. Beehive | Item | Honeycomb | Beehive | | --- | --- | --- | | Running mode | A desktop app installed on your own computer | Reached in a browser, in the cloud | | Data storage | Local (/.wunder) | Hull storage | | Interactive terminal | ✅ Yes | ❌ No | | Voice input / output | Input ✅, output ❌ | Both directions ✅ | | Tray / system notifications / global hotkey / screenshot | ✅ | ❌ | | Device-interconnection settings panel | Category not opened; only the cloud workspace + approval pop-up | ✅ Devices category + interconnection view | | One agent | Multiple threads, multiple workspaces | The same | Common questions Data location: the workspace is at /.wunder/workspace, sessions and tool logs are in a local database, and settings are at /config/desktop.settings.json; WUNDERHOME moves the root elsewhere. Local mode can still go online: "local-first" means the data stays on this machine; it does not affect access to remote models or web pages. Moving to another computer: copy the whole /.wunder folder (workspace, database, and settings). On the first launch it scans the work tree and restores the state of tasks that were queued, waiting, running, or cancelling. Creating threads while running: one agent can hold several independent task threads at once, with locks and realtime state isolated per thread; with the session queue on, new messages queue up instead of being rejected as "user busy". summary: The operating references and configuration notes you reach for most — where a feature lives, what a status means, and how to change a setting.
text: Reference Overview The operating references and configuration notes you reach for most — where a feature lives, what a status means, and how to change a setting. The pages below cover where a feature lives, what a status means, and how to change a setting. All pages Interfaces and endpoints Feature and Capability Quick Reference What wunder can do, and where each capability lives. Chat WebSocket The realtime channel is also the session-control channel: start, resume, watch, cancel, and returning approvals all ride on the same connection. WeChat iLink Channel Configuring the weixin channel, and how it differs from the legacy WeChat channel. Workspace Routing and File Management The single cloud directory, path conventions, and management tips. Session Status Guide What the various statuses during a chat mean. title: Chat WebSocket
summary: The real-time channel for chat and also the session control channel: starting an execution, resuming after a disconnect, watching, canceling, and returning approvals all happen on the same connection.
headings: What You Can Do on the Connection
text: Chat WebSocket The real-time channel for chat and also the session control channel: starting an execution, resuming after a disconnect, watching, canceling, and returning approvals all happen on the same connection. /wunder/chat/ws does more than push events to you; it is also the control channel for a session. Both chat and desktop real-time sessions use it, and there is no SSE fallback. Use Cases You are building a chat workbench or a desktop session. You need to start, resume, watch, and cancel an execution on the same connection. You need long-lived connection keepalive and consistent real-time state. Connecting 1. Create a session first and take note of its ID. 2. Open the WebSocket connection. 3. Send the connect handshake. 4. Receive ready. 5. Send start to begin an execution. 6. Keep consuming event until this round's terminal state, turnterminal. Handshake example: Starting an execution: What You Can Do on the Connection connect: handshake and protocol negotiation start: begin an execution resume: catch up on what was missed after a disconnect watch: observe a session without driving it cancel: cancel the current execution approval: return an approval decision ping: keepalive The server mainly returns ready, event, error, and pong. Key Settings and Common Pitfalls Watch these event categories in particular: queued, approval resolved, error, and end of turn. turnterminal is the terminal signal for a single execution round and works well as the frontend's convergence condition. start must explicitly carry the session ID. The body text uses content, not /wunder's question. resume (catching up on events) and watch (observing the runtime state) are two different actions. Approvals on this connection only handle approval items that come from the WebSocket. Handling a Disconnect Do not fall back to SSE. Reconnect to /wunder/chat/ws, then send as the situation requires: resume: carry the position of the last handled event to fill in the events missed during the disconnect. watch: observe the current session's runtime state again. Further Reading Stream Events Reference Use Cases Connecting What You Can Do on the Connection Key Settings and Common Pitfalls Handling a Disconnect Further Reading

title: MCP Endpoint
summary: wunder can both expose itself as an MCP service and act as an MCP client to connect to external services.
text: MCP Endpoint wunder can both expose itself as an MCP service and act as an MCP client to connect to external services. MCP has two directions: the MCP service wunder exposes to the outside; wunder acting as a client to connect to someone else's MCP service. Direction: Self-Hosted vs. External You want external systems to call wunder's capabilities over MCP → use the self-hosted side. You want to bring external capabilities in for the model to use → use the external-service side. Expose wunder The outward entry is a single address, served over Streamable HTTP. The order in which it comes together: 1. The external system connects to that address following the MCP protocol; 2. wunder negotiates the protocol version automatically; when it interoperates with an older service it settles on a version both sides support, so the initialization step does not have to be written by hand; 3. Call the specific tools. Two tools are built in for external callers: excute (execute) and doc2md (document to Markdown). The tool name is literally excute; call it by exactly that name. Connect an External MCP Declare the MCP service you want to connect in the configuration — give it a name, an address, and a transport — then switch it on. Once enabled, wunder treats it as a callable service. External services also use Streamable HTTP; if the service is written in Python, it negotiates according to the Python side's protocol version and may not carry every latest capability. A typical example is the external service often mentioned in the documentation, which usually hosts tools such as database query, database export, and knowledge-base query. Key Settings and Common Pitfalls Suggested integration order: declare the service in the configuration → confirm in Bridge that the tool list can be fetched → then expose it to the model. Bridge has MCP configuration and debugging entries where you can refresh the tool list and call remote tools directly to verify them. MCP tools are not a side channel: they are aggregated together with built-in tools, A2A tools, skills, knowledge-base tools, and self-built tools into one tool view. To the model, MCP is just part of the tool catalog. Further Reading Tool System Configuration Reference Direction: Self-Hosted vs. External Expose wunder Connect an External MCP Key Settings and Common Pitfalls Further Reading

title: WeChat iLink Channel
summary: The new WeChat channel uses the iLink protocol and is not the same thing as the legacy Official Account or WeCom channels.
text: WeChat iLink Channel The new WeChat channel uses the iLink protocol and is not the same thing as the legacy Official Account or WeCom channels. weixin is an independent channel, not an old WeChat channel with different parameters. Choosing a Channel | Scenario | Choose | | --- | --- | | Enterprise WeChat app callback | wechat (legacy) | | WeChat Official Account callback | wechatmp (legacy) | | WeChat capability over the iLink protocol | weixin (new) | The main differences between new and old: Inbound: weixin pulls updates by long polling; the legacy version uses Webhook callbacks. Reply requirement: a weixin reply must carry the context identifier of the current session; the legacy version does not depend on it. Login: weixin scans a QR code to obtain the bot token; the legacy version uses traditional enterprise / Official Account parameters. Media: weixin goes through a CDN and handles encryption and decryption itself; the legacy version goes through the platform's native interface. Status: prefer weixin for new integrations; the legacy version is in maintenance / compatibility mode for existing deployments. Connecting by QR Code After choosing weixin in the channel settings: 1. Click "Generate QR code"; 2. Scan it with WeChat; 3. Click "Wait for confirmation"; 4. The system fills in the bot token, bot ID, user ID, and interface address automatically; 5. Save the account configuration. Two notes: after the auto-fill, you must save for long polling to actually take effect; the QR code has a validity period and must be regenerated once it expires. Key Settings and Common Pitfalls Three required fields: interface address, bot token, and bot ID; then turn on the long-connection switch. A few optional enhancements remain: CDN address, bot type, allowed caller range, polling and interface timeouts, backoff after consecutive failures, and route tag. Media-link troubleshooting order: whether media is enabled, whether the CDN address is reachable, whether the decryption key is correct, and whether the attachment exceeds the size limit. A reply reporting "missing session context identifier" means the reply did not receive the context identifier from the previous inbound message. Confirm the reply goes through the same session and that the inbound message preserved it. Not receiving messages for a long time: check in order whether the account is active, whether the long connection is on, whether the token and bot ID are valid, and whether the session has expired in the Bridge runtime view. Sessions expiring frequently: usually the login state is lost; scan again for a new token and save. Migrating from the Old Channel 1. Run in parallel first: keep the old channel and let new traffic prefer weixin; 2. Switch over by account, in batches; 3. Watch inbound success rate, outbound success rate, first-packet latency, and the failure ranking; 4. Once stable, mark the old channel as maintenance mode. Further Reading API Index Admin Interface Choosing a Channel Connecting by QR Code Key Settings and Common Pitfalls Migrating from the Old Channel Further Reading

title: System Settings Reference
summary: What the common settings mean and what to set them to.
text: System Settings Reference What the common settings mean and what to set them to. ## Settings categories wunder's settings fall into a few broad categories by responsibility: Basic settings: service address, port, and run mode Security settings: access control and permission boundaries Storage settings: where and how data is stored Tool settings: which tools are available Model settings: AI model selection and parameters Channel settings: external platform access Basic settings Service address and port These decide the network address and port the wunder service listens on. For local use, the defaults are fine For a team deployment, set an address the team can reach Run mode This decides the form wunder runs in. Honeycomb local mode: suited to individual local use, with all data stored locally Hull mode: suited to teams and organizations, with multi-user support and centralized management Pick Honeycomb local mode for individual use; pick Hull mode when you need multi-user collaboration and centralized management. Concurrency limit This caps how many sessions can be active at once, so the system does not get overloaded. For individual use, the default is enough For team use, adjust it to the number of users and the available hardware Security settings API key This protects access to the Bridge and the Hull interfaces. A few points: The key should be long enough — over 16 characters, mixing letters, digits, and symbols Do not use a key that is easy to guess Rotate the key regularly Path access control This limits the file paths the agent may touch and the commands it may run. Allowed paths: the directories the agent may work in Denied patterns: the file types or paths that are off limits As a safety practice, do not open the whole filesystem: name the working directories the agent may use and block sensitive system directories. External auth key When wunder is embedded in another system, this key verifies incoming external requests. It fits cases such as calling wunder from another system or an embedded integration. Storage settings Database type This decides which database stores business data. SQLite: a lightweight local database, the default for Honeycomb local mode PostgreSQL: a full-scale database, suited to the Hull multi-user mode Workspace location This decides where user files and agent artifacts are stored. A few points: In Hull mode, make sure the workspace directory is persistent (use NAS or network storage) Do not put the workspace in a temporary directory Vector storage This is the storage backend used by knowledge-base retrieval, saved alongside the main storage backend: PostgreSQL in Hull mode and SQLite in Honeycomb local mode. Configure it when you need knowledge-base retrieval. Tool settings Built-in tool switches These control which built-in tools the agent may use. In sensitive environments, consider turning off command-execution tools and opening only what is actually needed. Browser tools These let the agent browse pages and take screenshots. Enable them directly for local use; a Hull deployment may need Docker container support. MCP extension tools These connect external tool services over the MCP protocol. Use them when you need specialized database operations, particular API calls, or third-party services. Model settings Available model list This decides which AI models the agent can choose from. Adding a model means supplying its API key and endpoint Different models have different billing and different strengths Offering several options lets users pick what fits Context limit This caps the conversation context so it stays within what the model handles. Setting it to the model's maximum is fine; when the limit is reached, the system compresses older content automatically. Channel settings Channel account binding This binds accounts on external platforms such as Feishu and WeCom. Create an app on the platform, obtain its credentials, and fill in the configuration for that channel type. Webhook configuration This lets an external platform push messages to wunder. Set up a publicly reachable receiving address and configure the webhook URL on the external platform. When configuration takes effect Timing of changes New settings: take effect for new sessions immediately Existing sessions: do not change; they keep the settings from when they were created Configuration layers System defaults: the bottom layer that any unset value falls back to Per-user settings: override the system defaults and affect only that user Agent settings: the top layer, affecting only that agent Order of precedence: agent settings > user settings > system defaults. Recommended configuration by scenario Individual local use (Honeycomb desktop) Database: SQLite (default) Workspace: a local directory Security: limit sensitive paths reasonably Tools: open them as needed Team collaboration (Hull server) Database: PostgreSQL Workspace: network storage (persistent) Security: configure keys and path limits strictly Tools: assign permissions by role Settings categories Basic settings Service address and port Run mode Concurrency limit Security settings API key Path access control External auth key Storage settings Database type Workspace location Vector storage Tool settings Built-in tool switches Browser tools MCP extension tools Model settings Available model list Context limit Channel settings Channel account binding Webhook configuration When configuration takes effect Timing of changes Configuration layers Recommended configuration by scenario Individual local use (Honeycomb desktop) Team collaboration (Hull server)

title: Workspace Routing and File Management
summary: Each user has a single cloud workspace directory. Paths are always workspace-relative, and the container parameter has been converged — directories are no longer derived per agent or container.
text: Workspace Routing and File Management Each user has a single cloud workspace directory. Paths are always workspace-relative, and the container parameter has been converged — directories are no longer derived per agent or container. Every user has a single cloud directory. One cloud directory per user Isolation has one layer only: by user. Each user's files live in their own single cloud directory, partitioned by the server under its data root. | Convention | Meaning | |------|------| | Unique | There is only one workspace directory at any time; opening more threads or subagents never adds another | | Fixed | You cannot add, delete, or replace the directory, and you cannot bind a folder on your machine | | Isolated | Path checks are bounded by the user root; out-of-bounds access is rejected | | Persistent | The workspace is persistent storage and is not cleaned up automatically | Routing rules Routing for /wunder/workspace: 1. The request carries the signed-in user's identity 2. The server resolves that user's workspace root 3. The entry is located under that root by the relative path in the request The container parameter has been converged: the historical containerid no longer selects a directory, and the server always resolves against the user root. The parameter is still accepted during the transition, but 0 and 1 produce the same result, and the front end no longer offers a container choice. No more per-agent roots: agentid only affects conversation and configuration binding, not directory derivation. Subagents do not get their own directory: a subagent is a temporary work unit created by the main agent and shares the same user directory. Path conventions The API takes and returns workspace-relative paths, for example docs/notes.md The root directory is written as an empty string Do not pass a machine absolute path, and never show a server absolute path in the front end Invalid or out-of-bounds names are rejected outright rather than silently redirected Workspace versus temporary directory | | Workspace | Temporary directory | |--|--------|----------| | Purpose | Long-lived files and task artifacts | Transit for uploads and downloads, and document-conversion intermediates | | Lifecycle | Persistent, never cleaned automatically | May be cleaned periodically | | Paths | Workspace-relative | A separate transit namespace | Keep files you need to keep in the workspace and transit files in the temporary directory. Usage statistics GET /wunder/workspace/stats returns a bare object whose fields include the file count, directory count, bytes used, whether the walk was truncated, and recently modified files: The walk is bounded; it ends early for very large directories, and a true truncated means the counts are a lower bound A null quotabytes means no quota is configured; the interface then shows only the used amount, with no quota denominator The working-directory overview card on the welcome page and the usage bar at the bottom of the left sidebar share this data File management essentials Browse: directories load lazily, fetching children only when expanded; large directories are paginated and rows are virtualized Upload: use the toolbar, or drag files onto the file-tree area; uploads are concurrency-limited and can be cancelled or retried Preview and edit: text, images, Office documents, and diagrams each have a preview or online-edit overlay Reference to chat: choose "Reference to chat" in a file row menu to bring the file into the composer; entries in the timeline link back to it Batch and archive: multi-select to delete in bulk or download an archive High-risk operations: deleting or clearing a directory needs a second confirmation; front-end confirmation never replaces server-side authorization Uploads and file types | Type | Handling | |------|------| | Documents (PDF, Word, Markdown, and so on) | Converted to text automatically for the agent to analyze | | Images (PNG, JPG, and so on) | The agent can view and analyze them directly | | Audio (MP3, WAV, and so on) | Transcribed to text automatically | | Video (MP4, and so on) | Frames are extracted at a set rate for analysis | | Code files | Files in various programming languages, which the agent can read directly | | Other | Stored as-is, and the agent can try to read them | Some files must be processed after upload (document-to-text, audio transcription, and so on), and the send button stays disabled until processing finishes. Further reading Workspaces and Working Directory — the isolation model One cloud directory per user Routing rules Path conventions Workspace versus temporary directory Usage statistics File management essentials Uploads and file types Further reading

title: Session Status Guide
summary: What the various statuses in a chat mean, what the agent is doing, and what to do when something goes wrong.
headings: Why the agent waits for approval
When the status display looks wrong
Seeing what the agent did recently
text: Session Status Guide What the various statuses in a chat mean, what the agent is doing, and what to do when something goes wrong. During a conversation the interface shows statuses such as thinking, calling a tool, compressing context, or retrying after an error. Status overview A conversation usually passes through these states from start to finish: Basic statuses Waiting Meaning: the request has been submitted and is queued for handling. When it appears: When the system is busy When several requests are running at once What to do: wait; it usually starts soon. Thinking Meaning: the agent is analyzing your request and preparing to answer or act. Understanding the problem and working out a plan takes time, so this is a normal state. Wait a moment rather than resending the same message. Running tools Meaning: the agent is using tools to carry out the task, such as reading a file, searching the web, or running code. Messages you may see: "Reading file…" "Searching…" "Running…" Complex tasks often need several tools working together, and the interface shows the progress. Done Meaning: the agent has finished and given its final answer. What you can do next: Follow up with another question Review the content or files it produced Start a new task Approval statuses Approval needed Meaning: the agent wants to perform an action that needs your confirmation, such as changing an important file or running a risky command. When it appears: The agent wants to change an important file The agent wants to run a sensitive command An approval mode is configured What you see: An approval popup or prompt A description of the action the agent wants to take What to do: Read the description carefully Decide whether to approve Click Approve to continue, or Reject to stop it Approval resolved Meaning: you have made a decision on the approval request. Two outcomes: Approved: the agent continues with the action Rejected: the agent drops it and may look for another approach Abnormal statuses Failed Meaning: the agent ran into a problem and could not finish the task. Possible causes: A file is missing or unreadable A network request failed A tool errored out The AI model service had a problem What to do: Read the error for the cause Adjust the request as it suggests, such as giving the right file path Retry Cancelled Meaning: the conversation was stopped, either by you or by the system. When it appears: You clicked Stop The system timed out and cancelled Some other deliberate stop What you can do next: Start the conversation again Review the record of what ran before the cancellation Stuck session Symptoms: it stays in one state for a long time with no progress. Possible causes: The network connection dropped The backend service had a problem Task handling timed out What to do: 1. Wait a few minutes first (sometimes processing just takes a while) 2. If it is genuinely stuck, click Stop 3. Use the reset work state option in settings to clear an abnormal state 4. If that still does not help, contact an administrator or see the troubleshooting guide Connection status Connected Meaning: the network connection to the backend service is fine. Disconnected Meaning: the network connection to the backend service has dropped. Symptoms: You cannot send new messages The status display looks wrong A "connection lost" notice appears What to do: Check your network Refresh the page or restart the app Wait for it to reconnect automatically Where status indicators appear In the chat interface, status appears in these places: Above the conversation: the overall status of the current session Beside a message bubble: the processing status of that message In the progress area: detailed progress of tool execution Common situations Why responses slow down Possible reasons: The task is complex and needs several steps The AI model service is responding slowly The system is under high load Wait rather than resending the same message. Why the agent waits for approval The action may be risky or affect important files. This is a safety mechanism that makes sure sensitive actions are confirmed. To see fewer approvals, talk to an administrator about adjusting the approval mode. When the status display looks wrong 1. Wait first and see whether it recovers on its own 2. Use the reset work state option 3. Refresh the page or restart the app 4. Check the troubleshooting guide Seeing what the agent did recently The lower or right part of the chat usually holds a run trace or a record of tool calls, showing which tools the agent used, which files it read, and what actions it performed. Further reading Troubleshooting Core Agent Loop Tool System Status overview Basic statuses Waiting Thinking Running tools Done Approval statuses Approval needed Approval resolved Abnormal statuses Failed Cancelled Stuck session Connection status Connected Disconnected Where status indicators appear Common situations Why responses slow down Why the agent waits for approval When the status display looks wrong Seeing what the agent did recently Further reading

title: Prompts and Personalization
summary: Customize the agent's role and answer style — pick a built-in template, or write your own.
headings: What a pack is made of
Why an existing conversation keeps its template
Different agents can use different templates
A Chinese template can still answer in English
text: Prompts and Personalization Customize the agent's role and answer style — pick a built-in template, or write your own. A prompt template sets the agent's role and answer style. Pick a built-in one, or write your own, and the agent works to that agreement. Prompt templates A prompt template is the agent's handbook. It defines: The role How to think and answer The working principles and limits How to use tools and skills Switch to another template and the agent's style and emphasis change with it. Built-in template packs wunder ships two built-in packs. Chinese pack (default-zh) Thinks and answers in Chinese Fits Chinese-language conversations The default Chinese assistant style English pack (default-en) Thinks and answers in English Fits English-language conversations The default English assistant style Pick the pack that matches the language the user mostly works in. What a pack is made of Each pack is assembled from several segments that together form the agent's complete handbook: | Segment | Purpose | |------|------| | Role | Defines who the agent is and what role it plays | | Engineering principles | Defines how it works and thinks | | Tool protocol | Defines how it uses tools | | Skill protocol | Defines how it invokes skills | | Memory | Defines how it uses long-term memory | | Extra notes | Additional instructions | Switching packs Switching in the interface 1. Go to Settings at the bottom of the left sidebar → Agent 2. Find the prompt template option 3. Choose the pack you want 4. Save When it takes effect New conversations: ones created after the switch use the new template Existing conversations: unchanged, keeping the template from when they were created Creating a custom template How to create one 1. In the template settings page, click New template pack 2. Pick a template to copy as the base (starting from a built-in one is recommended) 3. Edit the content of each segment 4. Save, and it is ready to use Editing tips Role segment: state the role, such as "coding assistant" or "data analysis expert" Engineering principles: set the answer style (concise or detailed, formal or casual) Tool protocol: usually leave it alone Extra notes: put your own specific requirements here Example: a coding assistant template The role segment might read: How templates layer The agent's final prompt is combined from several layers: 1. System template: the global base set by an administrator 2. User template: the pack the user picked 3. Agent settings: extra configuration for that particular agent An upper layer overrides a lower one, and anything missing falls back to the lower layer. Common situations Why an existing conversation keeps its template A conversation fixes its prompt when it is created and then keeps it frozen, so behavior stays consistent and does not shift partway through. Changing one conversation's prompt An existing conversation's prompt cannot be edited directly. Start a new conversation to use the new template, or copy the content you want to keep into a new conversation and continue there. Different agents can use different templates Each agent configures its template independently. Longer is not always better A template should state the key requirements clearly and avoid redundancy and contradiction; a long or self-contradictory one runs counter to that. A Chinese template can still answer in English The template only sets a default tendency; ask for English in the conversation and the agent will follow. Usage notes Start from a built-in template, then customize from there Create a separate pack for each scenario if you like State the key requirements clearly and keep it short Do not put contradictory requirements in the same template Review it occasionally and drop entries you no longer need Further reading Feature and Capability Quick Reference — where agent management lives Prompts and Skills Long-term Memory Prompt templates Built-in template packs Chinese pack (default-zh) English pack (default-en) What a pack is made of Switching packs Switching in the interface When it takes effect Creating a custom template How to create one Editing tips Example: a coding assistant template How templates layer Common situations Why an existing conversation keeps its template Changing one conversation's prompt Different agents can use different templates Longer is not always better A Chinese template can still answer in English Usage notes Further reading

title: Bridge Panel Guide
summary: What each panel in the Bridge manages and where its entry lives.
text: Bridge Panel Guide What each panel in the Bridge manages and where its entry lives. The Bridge is the administrator's workbench: configure the system, manage users, and watch how things are running. Panel groups at a glance System group Global configuration and status Agent group Model and capability configuration Debug group Testing and performance evaluation Documentation group User guide and interface reference System group Internal status Shows how the system is running, including active sessions, system load, and the state of key components. System settings Configures global parameters, including the service address and port, security settings, storage settings, and tool switches. Organization management Manages the organizational structure: create and manage organizations, their hierarchy, and their members. User management Manages user accounts: view the user list, create users, edit user details, and manage quota accounts (grant, deduct, set balance). Inside a user's settings, the quota actions are: Set the balance directly: overwrites the current balance, which is useful for correcting the recorded figure Grant quota: increases the balance and records the cumulative amount received Deduct quota: reduces the balance and records the cumulative amount consumed Administrator accounts are not subject to balance limits The online status in the user list is split by client: Beehive (web), Honeycomb (desktop), and Helm (command line). Agent group Model configuration Manages the AI models available: add a model by filling in its API key and endpoint, configure model parameters, and set the default model. Thread management Views and manages active threads: thread status, force-cancelling a thread, and viewing thread logs. Preset agents Manages preset agent templates (there can be several, and each user is bound one-to-one to one of them): Create, edit, and delete presets Configure a preset's tools, model, prompts, and the fields the user may customize View bound users and adjust bindings in bulk (bind, rebind, unbind); unbinding requires naming a new preset Sync to bound users' instances — sync only the fields a user has not customized, or force-overwrite everything, with a dry run that previews how many users are affected Tool management Manages the tools available: view the built-in tool list, configure external MCP tools, and set tool permissions. System prompts Manages the global prompt templates: view and edit system templates, switch the default template pack, and create new packs. Debug group Throughput testing Choose a model, a concurrency list, an input length, and an output length. Each run tests one concurrency level from the list in order and fires that many requests at once. The default concurrency list is 1,2,4,8, the default input is 8.2k tokens, and the default output is 128 tokens; the usual presets are kept, and you can also type any integer within range. Token counts are shown as k from 1,000 and as m from 100,000. History snapshots show the input usage actually measured by the API. The right side shows the aggregated input and output, the first-token latency, the generation speed, and the total time; the history curve plots concurrency on the horizontal axis and shows both overall and per-request speeds. Engines that support it receive a fixed-length output parameter; other endpoints may finish early, and the actual usage and the reason for ending are kept in the details. Tests create no sessions or thread logs and keep only the last 50 performance summaries. The details and curves separate overall prefill and generation speed, per-prefill speed, and per-generation speed; speeds are shown as k tok/s from 1,000 and as m tok/s from 100,000. Selecting history entries compares performance curves by concurrency; the vertical axis uses concurrency 1 as the 0% baseline and shows relative change, hovering reveals the measured speed, and you can reuse a configuration or export the selected data. For virtual models, model configuration offers fast, medium, and slow profiles, defaulting to fast: prefill at 2000 / 500 / 100 tokens/s and reasoning plus generation at 200 / 50 / 10 tokens/s. Random replies and throughput simulations both reason before generating content, and log replay uses the recorded reasoning within the configured capability and budget. Throughput tests default to reasoning equal to one quarter of the total output and can be tuned with the reasoning switch and budget; simulated records are tagged and grouped separately by profile. Simulated model capabilities With a virtual model selected in model configuration, you can set the maximum context, maximum output, vision, hearing, reasoning, and tool capabilities. Context and output left empty default to 128k and 4k. When the input (including tool definitions) plus the output budget exceeds the window, a context-overflow is reported. Turning off vision or hearing makes the corresponding media requests fail. Images and audio can each carry a per-item token count; this only simulates usage and time and does not recognize content. Replay follows the tool-calling mode: functioncall uses the native tool channel, toolcall uses the text protocol, and freeformcall falls back to native or text depending on the API mode. Tool names and arguments come straight from the log, so nothing has to be filled in by hand; tool execution still follows permissions and approvals, and replay continues to the next model round once results come back. Running out of log entries raises an error rather than repeating old calls. Synthetic replies do not initiate tools. An over-long output is marked as a length termination, incomplete tool arguments are not executed, and the reasoning capability and budget also apply to throughput tests. Performance testing Tests response performance with single-request latency measurement and performance sampling. Capability evaluation Evaluates an agent's capability level with task-completion quality assessment and capability regression tests. Debug panel Live debugging tools: real-time request tracing, tool-call logs, and error investigation. LSP Language service protocol debugging: code intelligence service status and LSP configuration validation. title: Interlink
summary: The Beehive, the Honeycomb, and the Helm share one presence state, see each other's workspaces, and control each other in both directions.
text: Interlink The Beehive, the Honeycomb, and the Helm share one presence state, see each other's workspaces, and control each other in both directions. Interlink connects the Beehive (web), the Honeycomb (desktop), and the Helm (cli) into one system: unified presence + cross-end workspace visibility + two-way remote control. Local devices open no public inbound entry point; all traffic is relayed through the Hull. The three endpoints and prerequisites | Name | Form | Role | |------|------|------| | Beehive | web | The cloud AI workbench, provided with the Hull, opened in a browser | | Honeycomb | desktop | The local AI workbench, the desktop form, with direct access to files on this machine | | Helm | cli | The manual local entry point, the command-line form | Prerequisites: 1. All three endpoints share the wunder-runtime engine and the wunder-core contract. 2. The local device has signed in to the Hull through the existing cloud connection scheme, and holds wund + deviceid. 3. The Hull is the sole authority for accounts, devices, quota, and policy. The four capabilities | ID | Capability | What it means | |------|------|------| | R1 | Unified presence | The Hull maintains a cross-end node directory, and the three endpoints share one state model — online / away / busy / reconnecting / offline — at second-level precision (local) and near-real-time precision (web) | | R2 | Workspace visibility | The local workspace appears in the Beehive as a shadow projection, projecting metadata summaries (thread directory, directory-tree summary, scheduled tasks, usage); file contents are not mirrored, and are pulled on demand over the interlink tunnel as the user acts | | R3 | Cloud controlling local | The Beehive can issue graded operations to online local nodes (query / session control / workspace write / tool execution); sensitive operations go through local human-in-the-loop approval, and everything is audited | | R4 | Local controlling cloud | The Honeycomb and the Helm treat the cloud as a symmetric node — browse the cloud workspace, send messages to cloud threads, read thread event streams; the Helm provides a scriptable command group | The unified state model: | State | Meaning | |------|------| | online | Online and idle | | busy | Online and executing | | away | Online but inactive | | reconnecting | Recovering from a dropped connection | | offline | Offline | How to use it Honeycomb (desktop) | Entry point | What it does | |------|------| | Settings → the device interlink category | Tunnel state, device table, cloud workspace browsing | | Remote command approval dialog | Polls the pending queue every 2s; approve / reject | | Sidebar thread source badge | Cloud / device | | Tunnel client | Hangs up as soon as the process starts | Beehive (web) | Entry point | What it does | |------|------| | Sidebar | Presented as "device as workspace": a device appears as a sidebar workspace row, and the directory falls into place as threads are clicked | | The "cloud / device" dropdown switcher | Removed | Helm (cli) | Entry point | What it does | |------|------| | The cloud subcommand group | devices / ws / send / watch / audit / approve | | cloud status | Combines four sections: interlink tunnel, pending approvals, other devices, cloud workspace usage | | cloud watch | Frame types are snapshot / delta / command / error / close | Security boundary | Boundary | Meaning | |------|------| | No public inbound entry point | Reverse tunnel: the local side only makes outbound connections, opens no listening port, and control traffic is delivered over the already-established link | | Least capability | Each class of remote operation is a declarative capability, read-only by default | | Explicit authorization | Write and execution classes require local user authorization, and an administrator can tighten it further in the Bridge | | Graded approval | Risk tiers L0–L3, see the table below | | Complete audit | Every remote operation forms a chain that can be inspected | | One-click shutdown | The kill switch is held by the user | Risk tiers: | Level | Operations covered | Approval | |------|------|------| | L0 read-only | node.summary / shadow.refresh / workspace.list\|search\|stat\|read / threads.list\|get | No approval needed | | L0+ | workspace.read:binary | No approval needed + audited | | L1 session | thread.create / thread.message / thread.cancel / thread.answer | Approval needed by default, can be lowered to none | | L2 workspace write | workspace.write\|mkdir\|move\|copy\|delete | Approval mandatory, cannot be lowered | | L3 execution | tool.exec (allow-listed commands) / agent.spawn | Approval mandatory + disabled for administrators by default, can be enabled | The two worth remembering most: L3 is off by default: tool.exec and agent.spawn are not in a device's capability set by default; approvals are never remembered; only a summary of the execution result is returned. L2 writes are backed up first: write operations are backed up to 工作区/.interlinkbackup/ / (the most recent 50 generations are kept), and the result reports the SHA256 before and after. Non-goals Local and cloud threads are not merged, and are not visible to each other. Interlink is remote operation, not data synchronization; a remote thread always exists on the other side marked as "remote". No full mirroring or two-way synchronization of workspace files — only metadata projection plus on-demand pull. No graphical remote control; control granularity stops at the engine and file APIs. No NAT hole-punching; all traffic is relayed through the Hull. The Honeycomb and the Helm do not interlink directly; local-to-local access always goes through the Hull. Cost | Metric | Measured | |------|------| | Idle tunnel CPU | 0.114% of a single core | | Idle window memory | Working set growth 0.18 MB (one-time +4.7 MB at link setup, counted separately) | The numbers come from the two-phase same-process sampling of scripts/interlink-bench/measure-idle.ps1 (one baseline phase and one tunnel phase, measuring the delta). title: Troubleshooting
summary: Cause and check points by symptom.
headings: Service Starts but Features Are Unavailable
Real-time Status Not Updating, No Intermediate Steps Visible
Tools Don't Appear or Can't Be Called
Attachment Uploaded but Can't Be Sent
New Thread Button Is Grayed Out
Help Manual Blank or Won't Open
Capturing a Performance Report for Chat Stutter
What to Include When Reporting an Issue
text: Troubleshooting Cause and check points by symptom. Find the cause by symptom. Health check 1. Make sure the service is running and the page opens. 2. Make sure you can sign in and your account and password are correct. 3. Make sure the model is configured correctly and the API key works. Find by Symptom Login Fails or Access Denied Check: Whether your username and password are correct Whether you used the wrong entry point for the Bridge and the Beehive Whether your account is disabled Configuration Changes Not Taking Effect Check: Whether you edited the right configuration file Whether the change needs a service restart Whether the running instance actually loaded the changed configuration Service Starts but Features Are Unavailable Check: Whether the database is connected properly Whether the external tool services (MCP, A2A) are online Whether the sandbox service is reachable Real-time Status Not Updating, No Intermediate Steps Visible Check: Whether your network connection is stable Whether WebSocket is being blocked by a firewall or proxy Whether it recovers after refreshing the page Tools Don't Appear or Can't Be Called Check: Whether the tool is enabled Whether the MCP / A2A service is running Whether the current agent has that tool mounted Whether it is waiting for approval and you missed the prompt Attachment Uploaded but Can't Be Sent Check: Whether the file type is supported (images, audio, video, common documents) Whether the file is still being processed (the send button stays disabled until processing finishes) Whether the workspace has write permission Password Recovery Click "Reset Password" on the login page. You only need: Username Email New password No old password is required, and you don't need to sign in first. Password Change Won't Save Check: Whether you entered your current password (changing a password while signed in always verifies the old one) Whether the new password and the confirmation match Whether the new password is the same as the current one New Thread Button Is Grayed Out The button is briefly disabled while a thread is being created or switched. Threads running in the background can still start or switch, and an existing unused empty thread is reused first. Session State Completely Messed Up Use "System Settings → Reset Working State". It will: Stop running sessions and tasks Rebuild clean threads It will not delete skills, knowledge bases, or other long-term assets. Microphone or Screenshot Button Unavailable Check: Whether you are in an environment that supports these features Whether the browser has been granted microphone/screen permission Whether the desktop bridge is working properly Help Manual Blank or Won't Open Check: Whether the docs site has been built Whether the reverse proxy is configured correctly for the /docs/ path Capturing a Performance Report for Chat Stutter Open "More → Settings → Performance Capture" and follow three steps: 1. Click "Start", then return to chat and reproduce the stutter while replying, scrolling, or switching pages. 2. Go back to settings and click "Download JSON"; the browser downloads the report directly, ready to attach to your issue report. 3. Click "Stop" to end capture. You can still download afterward; starting again creates a new report. No console or reload is needed to start. If you reload the page yourself, this tab keeps capturing and retains the statistics from before the reload, for up to 30 minutes. Browser metrics that aren't supported are marked unavailable. The report includes frame gaps, main-thread long tasks, slower input events, chat rendering and loading timings, periodically sampled DOM/memory peaks, and the browser and app versions. It excludes message bodies, call arguments, accounts, session identifiers, and file paths. Downloading doesn't end capture and doesn't upload any file. When you submit, add what you did and when the stutter happened. Total model reply time and Worker wait time are not the same as main-thread stutter, and the report lists them separately. Still Unresolved Continue with: Configuration Reference What to Include When Reporting an Issue Runtime form: desktop / server / cli Steps that reproduce the problem Key error messages Whether it involves subagents, MCP, A2A, etc. Health check Find by Symptom Login Fails or Access Denied Configuration Changes Not Taking Effect Service Starts but Features Are Unavailable Real-time Status Not Updating, No Intermediate Steps Visible Tools Don't Appear or Can't Be Called Attachment Uploaded but Can't Be Sent Password Recovery Password Change Won't Save New Thread Button Is Grayed Out Session State Completely Messed Up Microphone or Screenshot Button Unavailable Help Manual Blank or Won't Open Capturing a Performance Report for Chat Stutter Still Unresolved What to Include When Reporting an Issue

title: FAQ
summary: Common conclusions for using wunder, ahead of symptom-level troubleshooting.
headings: When the New Thread Button Is Disabled
Difference Between webfetch and the Browser Tool
Where to Look When Something Goes Wrong
text: FAQ Common conclusions for using wunder, ahead of symptom-level troubleshooting. ## Registration and Sign-in No registration is required. You can start a conversation under any name, and the system creates the matching identity automatically. Cost and Usage The token count is not the cost. It only reflects the context length of the current conversation, and the actual cost depends on your model provider's billing rules. Scope of Requirement Settings Requirements set at the start of a conversation are remembered and locked in. Later messages follow them, so you don't need to repeat them. When Memory Loads Long-term memory loads once, at the start of a conversation. It is not re-read on every turn. When the New Thread Button Is Disabled The button is briefly disabled while a thread is being created or switched. Threads already running in the background do not block a new thread, and an existing unused empty thread is reused first. Subagents A subagent is a temporary work unit the agent creates during a task, used to split off work that can proceed in parallel and get it done; once the result is returned to the main thread, the subagent is reclaimed. It is not a separate agent — on the user side there is always exactly one agent instance. Honeycomb and Hull Dependency Deploying the Hull is not required. The Honeycomb can run locally on its own. Deploy the Hull when you need multi-person collaboration and unified management. Changing Your Username and Password Go to "My Profile → Edit". Changing your password requires entering your current password. Password Recovery Click "Reset Password" on the login page. You only need your username, email, and a new password — no old password required. Cleanup of Uploaded Files Files in the temporary directory may be cleaned up. Keep important files in the workspace's persistent directory. Tool Visibility Possible causes: the tool is not enabled, the MCP/A2A service is not running, or the current agent does not have that tool mounted. Difference Between webfetch and the Browser Tool webfetch: grabs the main text content of a webpage The browser tool: operates a webpage like a real person (clicking, scrolling, filling forms) Where to Look When Something Goes Wrong Start with Troubleshooting.
