title: Glossary
summary: Core terms in wunder documentation, explained in plain language.
text: Glossary Core terms in wunder documentation, explained in plain language. ## Product and Form Names | Name | Short id | Meaning | |------|------|------| | wunder | wunder | The product itself, the umbrella term for the agent orchestration platform: hand a goal to the agent, and it breaks the task down, calls tools, and delivers results. | | Core | core | The foundation: configuration, authentication, storage, and execution policy. | | Engine | runtime | The execution layer: task orchestration, thread runtime, tools, channels, and gateway. The Honeycomb and the Helm depend on the Engine directly, not on the Hull. | | Hull | server | The user and agent management platform: the server form, aimed at teams and organizations, handling multi-user access, permissions, and channel access, and providing the Beehive. | | Bridge | bridge | The governance frontend: the system administrator's management interface for system configuration and for user and channel governance. | | Bridge node | bridge node | A channel bridging node: it carries channel account access and message routing and is managed uniformly by the backend, with no standalone frontend page today. Keep it distinct from the governance frontend "Bridge". | | Beehive | web | The cloud AI workbench: the web form provided with the Hull, which users open in a browser. | | Honeycomb | desktop | The local AI workbench: the desktop form, the default entry point for individual users, running locally with direct access to local files. | | Helm | cli | The manual local entry point: the command-line form, aimed at hands-on operation, developers, and automation scripts. | Hull, Bridge, Beehive, Honeycomb, and Helm name concrete forms of wunder; Core and Engine name the underlying layers. Keep the two groups separate. The first mention in the body pairs a form's display name with its short id — for example Hull (server), Honeycomb (desktop), Helm (cli). User Your identity marker. It can be a registered account or a temporary virtual name; the system recognizes both. Agent The AI role that executes tasks. An agent has its own model, tools, and prompt configuration. Every user has exactly one agent instance, generated from a 1:1 binding to an admin-side preset; there is no user-side entry point to create, delete, switch, or reorder agents, and only the fields a preset marks as customizable can be changed. Preset Agent An agent template maintained by the admin. There can be several presets, but each user binds exactly one of them, which generates that user's single agent instance. A preset update can be pushed to bound users as "sync uncustomized fields / force overwrite". Thread One continuous conversation. One agent can have several threads, and each thread maintains its own context independently. Subagent A temporary work unit the main agent creates during a task and reclaims once the task is done. It is not a separate agent, and not a second agent the user owns. Workspace Your persistent file space. Every user has exactly one workspace, which tools use as their root: in the Honeycomb (desktop) it is a persistent directory on your own machine, with direct read and write access to local files; in a Hull (server) deployment it is the single per-user directory under the server data root, reached through the Beehive. A workspace cannot be added, deleted, or replaced. Working Directory The workspace entry point in the UI: below the workspace in the left column of the web app, holding a file tree, a toolbar (upload / new / refresh / multi-select), a usage bar, and a preview overlay. It is not an operating-system file browser. User Turn Every message a user sends is one user turn. Model Turn Every action the model takes (thinking, calling a tool, replying) is one model turn. One user turn may contain several model turns. Skill A capability package for the model. It usually contains documentation, scripts, and resource files that let an agent handle specific types of tasks. MCP Model Context Protocol. A standard interface that lets wunder connect to external tool services. A2A An interoperability protocol between agents. It lets agents from different systems discover and collaborate with each other. Channel An external messaging path, such as Feishu, WeCom, QQ, or XMPP. Through channels, an agent can send and receive external messages. Token The basic unit by which a model processes text. The token count reflects the current conversation's context length and does not equal the actual cost. Context Compression When a conversation gets too long, the system automatically compresses the history so the model can keep working without losing key information. Long-term Memory Knowledge an agent remembers across conversations. You can add it manually, or let the system distill it automatically. Further Reading Sessions and Turns Workspaces and Working Directory Stream Events Reference Product and Form Names User Agent Preset Agent Thread Subagent Workspace Working Directory User Turn Model Turn Skill MCP A2A Channel Token Context Compression Long-term Memory Further Reading

title: Architecture
summary: All four forms share the same core and engine; real execution happens inside sessions, and the interface reads a bounded display view.
headings: Four forms, each with its own delivery surface
What the interface sees is a bounded view, not an execution snapshot
text: Architecture All four forms share the same core and engine; real execution happens inside sessions, and the interface reads a bounded display view. All four forms share the same core and engine; real execution happens inside sessions, and the interface reads a bounded display view. Four forms, each with its own delivery surface | Form | How it is delivered | Interface | | --- | --- | --- | | Honeycomb | A desktop app; the engine ships inside the local process and calls in-process by default without local HTTP | Native UI, compiled into the app | | Beehive | A web app; its build artifacts are served read-only by a separate web service, not hosted by the Hull itself | Single-page app | | Helm | A command-line program; when terminal conditions are not met it degrades to one-shot execution instead of the full-screen interactive interface | Terminal UI | | Hull | A server process, mounting Bridge and a few static directories | Bridge (no build step) | There is only one core and one engine; the four forms differ only at the access layer. What a message passes through From the moment you send a message to the moment the final reply is stored, the order is fixed: | Step | What it does | | --- | --- | | Access | The main chat channel takes the request and can submit, resume, observe, cancel, and approve it | | Admission | The session runtime decides whether to run it immediately or queue it — the single decision point for "dispatch or queue" | | Record the user round | A user round is allocated idempotently; this is the only write entry for the session record | | Prepare the request | Context, visible tools, and the system prompt are assembled, and a decision is made on whether to freeze | | Main loop | Every model call increments the model round by one | | Run tools | Policy and approval, hooks, timeouts, and budget come first, then the call is dispatched to the actual tool | | Final reply | Multiple refreshes within the same model round update the same visible output item and never append duplicate bubbles | | Real-time push | Emitting an event writes to the persistence layer synchronously, and subscribers are notified only after the write completes | Three places that are easy to mislocate: The status registry the interface queries for a session's current state is a different thing from the session runtime that actually runs execution. In-process wake signals only exist to accelerate; across multiple instances, correctness comes from polling convergence, not from them. The four phases of a tool — pre, execute, post, result — are only a descriptive model; hooks are off by default and are not part of the execution main chain. Data and storage Storage is split by purpose: thread logs, sessions, workspaces, memory fragments, and so on each form their own group, and the engine depends only on this set of interfaces without caring which database sits underneath. For the choice of database: with no configuration it is SQLite, and configured as PostgreSQL it runs on PostgreSQL. There is no version table and no migration-script directory. Tables are created idempotently on startup and new columns are detected at startup, so there is no such thing as migrating by version number. Every kind of record — sessions, round tails, workspaces, media attachments, memory fragments, knowledge vectors, users and quotas, channel bindings, interop shadows — is defined together. What the interface sees is a bounded view, not an execution snapshot What you see is a bounded display view, not a full history you can page through to the end, and not a complete snapshot of execution. | View | Per page | Cap | Response budget | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Chat page (one row per user round) | 12 | 20 | 128 KB | | Thread trace page (per entry) | 80 | 100 | 192 KB | | Body chunks | 8 KB per chunk | — | fetched on demand | The mechanisms that go with it: a write also produces a projection table and a truncated preview; when a projection is not ready it falls back to a bounded window over the source table; background rebuilds stay at no more than 1% duty cycle; and each change push fetches 200 items. Do not mistake the machinery that measures historical usage and budgets for context compression for a pagination module — it does not handle pagination. External interfaces | Surface | Fact | | --- | --- | | HTTP | Routes share the /wunder/ prefix, and error responses have exactly one source format | | WebSocket | Six channels: chat, the core request surface, gateway, interop tunnel, interop remote observer, and world / LAN | | Gateway | Not an HTTP gateway, but an access registry plus targeted RPC plus online-presence broadcast; its only transport is /wunder/gateway/ws | | Channels | Adapter registration; a bounded inbound queue, and a persistent outbound outbox with backoff retry | | Interop | Local nodes are outbound-only; one tunnel carries three planes; capabilities are tiered L0–L3, and the default device capability set excludes L3 | | MCP | The Hull has a built-in service endpoint at /wunder/mcp (streamable-http), and external MCP clients are registered in configuration | Runtime defaults | Item | Default | | --- | --- | | Hull listen | 0.0.0.0:8000, overridable by environment variable or configuration | | Active session cap | 300 (unlimited for administrators) | | Session lock | 120 s timeout, 5 s heartbeat | | Model / tool timeout | 120 s each | | Model round cap | 1000 for non-administrators | Common misconceptions "The Beehive page is hosted by the Hull." No. The Hull mounts only Bridge and a few static directories; Beehive's build artifacts are served by a separate web service. "The front end needs several fetches to get the full history." The front end was never meant to get the full history; it consumes a paginated view and fetches body chunks on demand. "Honeycomb calls its own backend over local HTTP." By default it is a native in-process call; the standalone compatibility bridge is kept only for existing clients. "Swarm orchestration is still part of the architecture." The engine and scheduling surface no longer have this module; only an empty directory remains, and session write permission is always writable. Further reading Agent Loop — the main loop and braking Sessions and Rounds — the numbering conventions Streaming Execution — push, refill, and backpressure Workspaces and Working Directories — paths and sandbox boundaries Configuration Reference — every configuration option Four forms, each with its own delivery surface What a message passes through Data and storage What the interface sees is a bounded view, not an execution snapshot External interfaces Runtime defaults Common misconceptions Further reading

title: Agent Loop
summary: You state the goal once and the engine runs the remaining steps; the loop advances round by round until it reaches a deliverable result or hits a brake.
headings: When it stops on its own
The thread is the unit of execution
When to wait, when to step in, when to open a new thread
text: Agent Loop You state the goal once and the engine runs the remaining steps; the loop advances round by round until it reaches a deliverable result or hits a brake. You state the goal once and the in-between steps need no human steering. It is not a question-and-answer exchange; the engine calls the model again and again, and each call can run a batch of tools, until it reaches a deliverable result or hits an explicit brake. How the loop runs A task starts with admission, and the engine enters the main loop. Each model round does three things: first it checks whether it should yield and whether the round cap has been exceeded, compressing the context when necessary; then it calls the model and gets back a piece of text or a batch of tool calls; if there are tool calls, it runs them in parallel or exclusively, writes the results back into the history as observations, and moves to the next round; if there are no tool calls, or a brake is hit, the round lands and the loop exits. The granularity follows Sessions and Rounds: One model round is one model call by the engine. A single round can contain several tool calls, and tool calls are not counted as separate rounds. Each round corresponds to one visible output in the interface; a tool batch is a separate entry in the timeline but is not a separate round. When it stops on its own The loop does not run forever; several guardrails bring it to a halt: Model round cap: non-administrator accounts default to at most 1000 rounds, and it stops once they are used up. Per-round tool-call budget: at most 10000 tool calls in a round; memory recall 2000 and library-query calls 2000 (relaxable to 10000 when necessary), and calls of a type beyond its limit are rejected. Repeated-failure circuit breaker: it stops when the same failure fingerprint recurs — 5 times for non-retryable errors, 2 times for parameter or protocol errors, and 4 times for "succeeded without progress"; after stopping it relays the failure reason to you. Context-overflow self-healing: at most 8 recovery attempts, each doing a corrective compression first and then retrying. Empty-output protection: one automatic retry (resampling with reasoning effort turned off); if it is still empty, it errors out and stops. Timeouts: model and tools default to 120 s each, with an additional idle watchdog; a timeout counts as a failure toward the circuit breaker. Session lock: the same thread runs serially, with a lock TTL of 120 s and a 5 s heartbeat; if the holder exits abnormally, the TTL releases it. Active-session cap: non-administrators are limited to 300, and beyond that requests queue or are told to try again later. Tool parallelism: at most 4; read-only tools run in parallel and exclusive tools run serially. Approval and risk tiering are independent of the loop: write or execute calls suspend and wait for your decision, and approval results are cached by tool category for 600 s so the same kind of operation is not asked about again and again. Where each round lands Every round of the loop must finally land on a result, which the interface state reflects: Completed normally: a deliverable reply is produced. Rejected: the request was not admitted (busy, quota exhausted, invalid request). Cancelled: you stopped it yourself. Failed: the execution errored (tool guardrail, no-progress guard, model error). While it waits for your input or for an approval, the thread is not in a terminal state; it is still within its lifetime. The thread is the unit of execution An agent can hold several independent task threads at once; scheduling, locking, and real-time state are all isolated per thread, and different threads do not block one another. Once a thread is set, the system prompt is frozen and long-term memory is injected only once at initialization and never rewritten afterwards. This keeps long tasks behaviorally stable and lets the model-side cache be reused. A subagent is a unit of work the main agent creates on the fly; it runs its own loop, passes results back to the parent thread, and is reclaimed when the task ends. This is the only form of collaboration. When to wait, when to step in, when to open a new thread Wait when you see "running tool" or several tool entries appearing one after another, which means the loop is advancing normally. Sending the same sentence again does not speed it up; it only queues another user round. Step in when: An approval pops up, so decide whether to approve or reject. The inquiry panel asks, and the thread moves to waiting for human input. The direction is wrong, so add an instruction, and the new user round carries the new context. There has been no output for a long time while the state is still running, so stop it and restate the goal. Open a new thread when the topic changes, the context is already very long, or you need a clean prompt base (after you change an agent's setup or memory, only a new thread picks it up). A few clarifications The claim that every tool call counts as a round is wrong — a tool batch belongs to the same model round. The loop does not retry without limit; repeated failures, progress-free successes, overruns, and empty output all have circuit breakers. A still interface does not mean the loop has stopped; check the state first: waiting for approval, waiting for input, and queued are all still within the lifetime. Streaming output is only a way of presenting things; the truth of the loop is in the thread ledger — see Streaming Execution. A subagent does not share the parent thread's context; it is an independent thread with an independent loop, interacting only through callbacks and a mailbox. title: Tools
summary: The agent's ability to act comes from a four-layer structure: executor tools, skills that package callable knowledge and scripts, capabilities the administrator selects, and tools the user connects. Keeping the layers distinct is what keeps "selectable" separate from "invokable".
headings: Dynamic registration: the model sees more than the built-in list
Result trimming runs on two tracks
text: Tools The agent's ability to act comes from a four-layer structure: executor tools, skills that package callable knowledge and scripts, capabilities the administrator selects, and tools the user connects. Keeping the layers distinct is what keeps "selectable" separate from "invokable". The agent's ability to act is collectively called "tools," but tools, skills, capabilities, and user tools are four different layers, and conflating them is the most common cause of broken configuration. Tools layer diagram: tool description, execution layer, model input results, and display projection—four related layers The four layers | Layer | What it is | Who uses it | How to tell | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Tool | Executor: one call reads a file, runs a command, or sends a request | The model calls it directly; the engine dispatches and runs it | Registered in the tool catalog and carries a dispatch branch | | Skill | Knowledge-and-script package: a directory holding the SKILL.md body and an entry script | The model can call it by skill name, or read the body through the skill-call action | Registered in the skill catalog | | Capability | Selection unit on the governance side: a unified descriptor an administrator uses to choose what an agent may use | Configured on the admin side; never enters the execution chain | Its source is built-in, MCP, skill, knowledge base, user MCP, user skill, user knowledge base, or shared | | User tool | An extension the user connects, in three kinds: MCP, skill, knowledge base | Mounted per user; the alias enters the routing table | Registered in the user tool catalog | Tools are executors; skills are callable knowledge and scripts; capabilities are the administrator's selection layer; user tools are the three kinds of user-side connection. A capability being selected does not mean an executor exists, and an executor existing does not mean the model can see it. Names: canonical name plus alias Most of the tool names the model sees are Chinese canonical names, with English aliases alongside, and a normalization pass runs before every invocation. | Canonical | Common aliases | Canonical | Common aliases | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 执行命令 | executecommand | 读取文件 | readfile | | 命令会话 | commandsession, writecommandstdin | 写入文件 | writefile | | ptc | programmatictoolcall | 文本编辑 | edit, patch, applypatch, 应用补丁 | | 列出文件 | listfiles | 搜索内容 | searchcontent | | glob | — | 技能调用 | skillcall, skillget | | 计划面板 | updateplan | 问询面板 | questionpanel, askpanel | | 定时任务 | scheduletask | 记忆管理 | memorymanager, memorymanage | | 子智能体控制 | subagentcontrol | 网页抓取 | webfetch | When a tool is written down in configuration, logs, or documentation, give both the canonical name and the alias; writing only one makes the two easy to mismatch. Dynamic registration: the model sees more than the built-in list The names that enter the model's tool list are assembled from four kinds of dynamic registration. | Source | Name on the model side | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | | MCP server | server@tool | Registered tool by tool; on a name clash the display name gains a server-name or hash suffix | | Packed MCP | server@mcppack | A server marked as packed folds into a single tool whose actions are list, get, and call | | Skill | The skill name itself | A skill name can be called directly; the skill-call action reads the body and substitutes the skill root-path placeholder | | Knowledge base | The knowledge base name | Registered one base at a time, replacing the old single knowledge tool | | User-tool alias | The alias | Dispatch routes by alias first; a hit goes straight to the user tool | Dispatch order is alias → skill → MCP → knowledge base → built-in tools, and a hit earlier in the chain short-circuits the rest. Defaults and per-form differences Default tool sets, the desktop hidden set, and the desktop extra set all have a single registration; do not keep a second copy in the docs or the configuration. | Set | Contents | | --- | --- | | Default built-ins (13) | 定时任务, 记忆管理, 执行命令, 命令会话, ptc, 列出文件, glob, 搜索内容, 读取文件, 网页抓取, 技能调用, 写入文件, 文本编辑 | | Default skill | 技能创建器 | | Desktop hidden (neither selectable nor on by default) | getgoal, creategoal, updategoal (injected automatically by the runtime per session), 会话线程控制, 会话让出 | | Desktop extras, on by default | 读图工具, 桌面监视器, 桌面控制器, 子智能体控制 | 网页搜索 and ptc are temporarily withdrawn, not deleted: the code is kept and dispatch still recognizes them, but the availability check returns unavailable for both, so neither the model nor the user can see them. To restore them, remove the matching entries from the withdrawal list. Visibility also runs through a few real gates. | Gate | Effect | | --- | --- | | The model has no vision | Filters out 读图工具 and the desktop tools | | The matching model or service is not configured | Speech generation, speech-to-text, image generation, and video generation each go unavailable | | Configuration not enabled | 网页抓取, 网页搜索, the 17 native browser tools, and the desktop tools | | Form | The desktop form filters out the hidden set | Browser is not a single tool: once enabled it registers 17 native tools named browser, and the aggregate display name "Browser" is only a documentation convention. Result trimming runs on two tracks Display trimming and model-input trimming are separate and do not affect each other. | Track | Rule | Affects | | --- | --- | --- | | Display | A preview of at most 2,400 characters or 16 lines, with an ellipsis past that | Only the client display; the raw result is kept in full and can be copied | | Model input | Trimmed by budget, with reproducible old observations compressed | What the model sees at the next step | Seeing "…" in the UI does not mean the model sees that same truncated copy; and when the model's context has been compressed to a preview, the UI may still show the full content. To judge context pressure, look at the compression page and the usage page, not the collapsing in the UI. Approval tiers Approvals are filed by the tool's risk category, and there are four categories: read-only, file write, running a command or a script, and controlling host capabilities. Pending requests are registered in two kinds by source: chat connection and channel. The cache that lets one approval cover a short window lasts 600 seconds within the same session. Execution policy has three states: allow, audit, and enforce; under enforce, high-risk actions must have human approval. A front-end confirmation cannot replace back-end authorization. Further reading Tool System — the dispatch chain, trimming constants, and protocol differences Tools Overview — arguments and usage for each tool Context Compression — how the model-input track saves tokens Prompts and Skills — SKILL.md and skill injection Multi-user and Capability Management — how administrators choose capabilities Configuration Reference — tool- and capability-related settings The four layers Names: canonical name plus alias Dynamic registration: the model sees more than the built-in list Defaults and per-form differences Result trimming runs on two tracks Approval tiers Further reading

title: Tool System
summary: The full path a tool takes from registration and selection through dispatch to its result landing, along with parallelism, timeouts, budgets, and clipping conventions.
headings: The path of one tool call
text: Tool System The full path a tool takes from registration and selection through dispatch to its result landing, along with parallelism, timeouts, budgets, and clipping conventions. Layered concepts, the default set, and naming conventions live in Tools (core concepts), and per-tool usage is in the Tools overview. The path of one tool call Two points are easy to get wrong: The four stages "pre → execute → post → result" only describe the model; hooks are off by default and are not the main execution chain. A business failure is not raised as an error in the dispatch layer but returned as a normal path. "The tool returned but the business did not succeed" is normal, and the model reads the reason for the failure. Why a tool is "invisible" | Where it is stuck | Criterion | | --- | --- | | Not registered | The name is not in the canonical-name / alias table, and no matching MCP, skill, or knowledge base exists | | Temporarily withdrawn | Web search and ptc: the code is still there but they are invisible in every case | | Not in the capability selection layer | The administrator has not selected that capability for this agent | | Filtered by form | Desktop mode hides target-management actions and session thread control / session yield | | Filtered by a capability threshold | Without vision, image reading and desktop tools are filtered out; the multimodal set needs a matching model; web fetching / browser need configuration enabled first | | Name short-circuited | When an alias and a skill share a name, the earlier route matches first | Naming and dynamic registration MCP tools are named "server @ tool"; a package-enabled server folds into a single tool operated through three actions: list, get detail, and call. When a tool name collides across servers, a server-name segment is appended; a collision within one server adds a runtime suffix. A skill name can be called directly; a knowledge base is registered library by library, and there is no single "knowledge base" tool. A user-defined tool alias enters the alias table and is routed by alias first during dispatch. Parallelism, timeouts, and budgets | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Parallelism ceiling | 4 | | Parallel decision | Whether a batch of tool calls can run in parallel is decided in the orchestration layer | | Lock semantics | A parallelizable tool takes a read lock; an exclusive tool takes a write lock | | Default tool timeout | 120 seconds (minimum 1 second) | | Tool-call budget | 10000 per round | | Memory-recall budget | 2000 per round | Tools outside the parallelism allowlist run serially, deliberately: write and execution tools are exclusive. Two clipping channels for results | Channel | Behavior | Impact | | --- | --- | --- | | Display | Preview 2400 characters and 16 lines, with an ellipsis beyond that | Affects client rendering only; the original message and copied content stay complete | | Model input | Truncate head and tail by budget; older reproducible observations go to micro-compaction | Decides what the model sees next | The budget into the model: 10000 characters at each of head and tail; arrays at most 128 items (48 head + 16 tail); paged results 500 items (180 head + 60 tail). Clipping adds a "truncated" marker, so the model can see that content was cut. Micro-compaction conventions: keep the most recent 5 groups, collapse older observations into a 768-byte preview, and only act when at least 256 tokens are saved. MCP integration An external MCP client must be configured with a name, endpoint, transport, request headers, authentication, allowed tools, whether to package, and tool specs. The hull's built-in MCP service endpoint is /wunder/mcp (streamable-http), exposing two tools, wunder@excute and doc2md; it returns 501 when the matching capability is off. The standalone Python FastMCP service carries its own configuration and toolset and is not part of this engine. The protocol follows the provider The tool-call protocol is decided by the provider: | Situation | Mode | | --- | --- | | The model explicitly configures a tool-call mode | Follow the configuration | | The provider is openai | Text-protocol tool calls | | Any other provider | Native function calls | | An unrecognized value | Fall back to the tag / xml text protocol | The text protocol's lark syntax is currently reserved for the patch form of text editing; parameter repair and nested restoration happen in the core library. There is no separate tool-protocol branch for Win7; the confirmed difference is only on the interop side — an older Win7 node does not declare the "execute command" capability. Removed and merged | Status | Item | | --- | --- | | Removed | User-world tools, channel tools, a2a tools, finalresponse, a2ui tools, LSP query / node-call tools, and the standalone sleep-and-wait tool | | Merged | applypatch merged into text editing (one tool with three forms: replace / patch / subcommand) | | Semantics changed | Session yield replaces the old sleep-and-wait | | Temporarily withdrawn | Web search and ptc (code kept, invisible) | Common mistakes The four-stage model is not the main execution chain, and hooks are off by default. A clipped result does not mean the model cannot see it: the display channel and the model input channel are separate. More tools do not make the agent smarter; quite the opposite: many names and vague descriptions raise the error rate, so the default set is deliberately restrained. A tool error is not a failed call: a business failure is returned to the model as a normal result with a reason and a next-step hint. Not every tool can run in parallel: only reads on the parallelism allowlist can, while writes and executions are exclusive. Win7 has no tool-protocol fallback branch. Further reading Tools (core concepts) — the four-layer model and the default set Tools overview — parameter documentation for each tool Context compression — micro-compaction and history compression Real-time behavior — how tool events are pushed to the client Stability — timeouts, budgets, and circuit breaking Configuration reference — MCP and tool toggle settings The path of one tool call Why a tool is "invisible" Naming and dynamic registration Parallelism, timeouts, and budgets Two clipping channels for results MCP integration The protocol follows the provider Removed and merged Common mistakes Further reading

title: Realtime
summary: The realtime channel runs on WebSocket; a reconnect catches up by cursor; what the client sees is a projection of backend truth; slow clients are uncoupled to protect the stream.
headings: The backend is truth, the frontend is a projection
Chat streaming runs only over WebSocket
Display reads are bounded and paged
text: Realtime The realtime channel runs on WebSocket; a reconnect catches up by cursor; what the client sees is a projection of backend truth; slow clients are uncoupled to protect the stream. Realtime is not about text appearing quickly but about three things: the process stays visible, a disconnect can be caught up on, and what the client sees matches backend truth. The approach is durable events, cursor-based catch-up, and a bounded projection — not hoping a reconnect happens to work. Realtime diagram: thread facts projected to client state through event streams and recovery mechanisms The backend is truth, the frontend is a projection The thread log is the single source of truth. Every event push is written synchronously to the persistence layer first, and only then travels the realtime channel. The change wake-up signal only wakes subscribers; it is not a data source, and not the truth. Three things follow directly: A dropped push can be recovered; the truth cannot be lost. When the interface shows something odd, trust the actual execution state — do not decide from the UI whether a task has finished. To tell whether a turn has ended, look only at terminal events, not at "it seems to have gone quiet". Chat streaming runs only over WebSocket Streaming chat output runs only over WebSocket. Requesting the chat stream over HTTP is rejected with a message pointing you to /wunder/chat/ws. SSE is for external workflows only and is not a fallback for chat. WebSocket endpoints are distributed by purpose: | Endpoint | Purpose | | --- | --- | | /wunder/chat/ws | Main channel for the thread runtime: connect, heartbeat, start, resume, subscribe, and cancel, plus goal-type and approval-type messages | | /wunder/ws | Core request surface: request submission and streaming responses | | /wunder/gateway/ws | The gateway's three roles (operator, node, channel): request/response/event/heartbeat | | /wunder/interlink/ws (paired with POST /wunder/interlink/channelticket) | Local node reverse tunnel | | /wunder/interlink/remotews | A browser observing a remote single thread; forwarding only, nothing persisted | | /wunder/userworld/ws, /wunder/desktop/lan/ws | Subscribing to and sending world-session messages; LAN networking | Handshake and authentication: send a connection envelope first, or pass accesstoken / token directly as a query parameter. Any other message before the handshake completes is rejected. The events you receive Event names are not enumerated in one place — each is declared where it is sent, and a new one is added the same way. The events that currently exist fall into these categories by purpose: | Category | Events | | --- | --- | | Projection and catch-up | threadviewchange, threadviewrequired, threadsnapshotrequired, threadstatus | | Thread content | threaditemtail, threaditemdelta | | Model output | llmoutputdelta, llmrequest | | Tools | toolcall, toolresult | | Queueing | queueenter, queueupdate, queuestart, queuefinish, queuefail | | Usage and quota | modelrequestusage | | Terminal state | final, turnterminal | | Flow control and errors | heartbeat, slowclient, streamoverflow, error; resumerecommended is emitted together with slowclient or streamoverflow | How a reconnect catches up The right way to reconnect after a disconnect is not to pull everything again, but to catch up with cursors. Three cursors each cover a different span: | Cursor | Meaning | | --- | --- | | changeseq | The thread-change sequence; a request passes afterchangeseq to say where to start catching up | | viewseq | The display-projection sequence; the client uses it to tell whether its local projection is behind | | eventseq / eventid | The sequence number of a single event, sent along with the event | Catch-up goes over HTTP endpoints with the same authentication as the user side: a session's thread-log changes, snapshot, and events (/wunder/chat/sessions/{id}/thread-log/changes|snapshot|events), and the display projection's bootstrap, chat, trajectory, changes, and search (/wunder/chat/sessions/{id}/view/bootstrap|chat|trajectory|changes|search). The consumer always fetches 200 changes at a time and immediately continues to the next page once a page is full. Submission is idempotent: include a clientmessageid, and a repeated submission is simply judged "accepted" and returns the original result. Re-sending the same message after a reconnect does not write it twice. Backpressure and bounds The realtime channel is bounded everywhere; the key values are: | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Per-subscription write queue | 256 | | Slow-client watermark | judged slow when queue remaining ≤ 2 | | Single-fetch cap | 200 | | Heartbeat interval | 15 seconds | | Single message cap | 512 KiB (256 KiB for interlink remote view) | | User input cap | 1,048,576 characters (image attachments not counted) | A slow client is handled by notifying first, then uncoupling: when the write queue crosses the watermark, a slowclient or streamoverflow is sent first along with resumerecommended, and the subscription is then dropped. This is not a failure but protection — better for one lagging subscription to exit and rebuild through catch-up than for a slow client to drag down the whole stream and the engine. The right reaction to a resumerecommended: rebuild the projection through the catch-up endpoints above, then re-subscribe with the new cursor, rather than waiting for the same connection to bring back what was missed. Display reads are bounded and paged For threads with a lot of data, the timeline and trajectory are not pulled in one shot; they are paged and given a response budget: | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | Chat page size / cap | 12 / 20 | | Trajectory page size / cap | 80 / 100 | | Response budget | 128 KB for chat, 192 KB for trajectory | | Body chunking | 8192 bytes | While the projection is not ready, reads fall back to a bounded window over the source table: the page size is clipped to the cap and then to the response budget. Background rebuilds have a duty-cycle cap (no more than 1%, backing off from 5 seconds to 300 seconds after a failure), so a thread that was just imported or heavily changed may still read from the source table for a short while — showing up as a slightly slower first screen, not as missing data. Thread listing pagination caps at 100, and keyword search scans at most 10 pages × 100, that is 1000 entries; anything beyond that is not found. This is a deliberate latency cap. Interlink: the other realtime path The realtime surface between local devices (Honeycomb, Helm) and the cloud is interlink, which differs from the client WebSocket above: Local nodes are outbound-only: they open no listening port. The local side initiates a single long connection, and the control, data, and command planes all share it. Shadow projection: the cloud holds a projection of the local threads and workspace directories. Writes are gated on a live channel; once the channel expires, no new shadow is written. Command ledger and approvals: commands, confirmations, events, and results are all recorded. Risk is tiered L0–L3; tool.exec and agent.spawn are L3, the default device capability set excludes L3, and L3 approvals cannot be remembered. Interlink governance currently exposes only backend interfaces; the Bridge has no interlink panel. Details and protocol are in Interlink. Further reading Streaming Execution — token increments and coalescing cadence Stability — timeouts, circuit breaking, and resource governance Stream Events — detailed meanings of states and events Chat WebSocket — handshake and message format Interlink — tunnels, shadows, commands, and approvals The backend is truth, the frontend is a projection Chat streaming runs only over WebSocket The events you receive How a reconnect catches up Backpressure and bounds Display reads are bounded and paged Interlink: the other realtime path Further reading

title: Stability
summary: Errors that do not spread, failures that can recover, and problems that can be reviewed. Stability comes from four kinds of hard constraint — bounds, budgets, circuit breaking, and a single writer — plus a consistent error structure and clear actions when something goes wrong.
headings: Every queue is bounded, and a full queue reports busy
Session locks and the single writer
What an error looks like from the outside
Whether to wait or to act
text: Stability Errors that do not spread, failures that can recover, and problems that can be reviewed. Stability comes from four kinds of hard constraint — bounds, budgets, circuit breaking, and a single writer — plus a consistent error structure and clear actions when something goes wrong. Stability rests on three things: containing the spread (one failing link does not bring down the others), being able to recover (failures have a formal recovery path), and being able to review (errors are structured and classifiable). It comes down to four kinds of hard constraint: bounds, budgets, circuit breaking, and a single writer. Stability diagram: risk sources pass through isolation governance and recovery paths to prevent cascading failures and form a regressable system Every queue is bounded, and a full queue reports busy Every queue has a fixed capacity. A write that fails and times out returns "queue busy" and records a busy metric. There is no unbounded buffer and no silent drop. | Queue | Bound | | --- | --- | | Per-subscription event write queue | 256 | | Slow-client watermark | remaining capacity ≤ 2 | | Single event fetch | 200 | | Thread changes per page | 200 | | Channel ingress | capacity 512 / concurrency 8 / enqueue wait 80 ms | | Workspace write queue | 2048 | Background tasks all start with a tag; a long run raises an alert, and one loop crashing does not take down the process. When troubleshooting, the task tag in the logs tells you which loop it was. Limits and budgets | Item | Value | | --- | --- | | User input cap | 1,048,576 characters; image attachments not counted | | Default model call timeout | 120 seconds | | Default tool timeout | 120 seconds (floor of 1 second) | | Tool concurrency | ≤ 4 | | Turn cap | 1000 by default for non-admins (floor of 2) | | Tool-call budget per turn | 10000 | | Memory-recall budget per turn | 2000 | | Session lock lifetime / heartbeat | 120 seconds / 5 seconds | | Active session cap | 300 by default (constrains non-admins) | | Approval cache | 600 seconds | Session queueing is on by default. With it turned off, sending a message while a run is in progress is immediately judged "user busy" and no queue entry is created either (the Hull warns about this at startup). This is a configuration trade-off, not a failure. Session locks and the single writer The same task thread executes serially, and different threads do not block each other: scheduling, locking, and realtime state are all isolated per thread. A session lock is a persistent lock with a 120-second lifetime, renewed by a heartbeat every 5 seconds. Waiters back off rather than polling on a fixed interval: backoff starts after two attempts, is capped at 3 seconds, and includes jitter; a wait longer than 30 seconds raises an alert. A fixed 0.2-second poll is deliberately avoided here, since a saturated system would otherwise turn its own polling into a storage storm. The single-writer principle: the thread log has exactly one write path. On submission: 1. Each session first passes through a gate that serializes it, so change order matches submission order; 2. The storage call is one short blocking transaction; 3. The cursor is published to the change channel only after the transaction succeeds — the channel carries a wake-up signal, not the truth; 4. Idempotent no-ops (a replayed acceptance, an unchanged state, duplicate feedback) produce no change and no notification; a failed submission never publishes a cursor. Callers must not assemble their own cursors, and must not notify the change channel before the transaction completes. This principle keeps "the order the client sees" consistent with "the order written to storage", and it is what makes lossless catch-up possible after a disconnect. Long-held locks and slow clients are two problems called out for governance: a lock is covered by its lifetime plus heartbeat in case the holder disappears, and a slow client is detected by the watermark, sent a resumerecommended first, and then uncoupled (see Realtime). Recovery and circuit breaking | Scenario | Mechanism | | --- | --- | | Streaming stalls | The idle watchdog judges by how long there has been no activity, not by total elapsed time | | The model returns empty or unusable output | Retried once with thinking off; if it still fails, an output error is reported | | Context over its limit | Progressive compression (triggered at three points: history, overflow, and pre-sampling); overflow recovery at most 8 times | | The same kind of failure recurring | Circuit broken by failure fingerprint | | Network or subscription disconnect | Cursor catch-up, without replaying the whole history | Retry circuit breaking counts by the same fingerprint; the thresholds are: | Condition | Threshold | | --- | --- | | Non-retryable failure | 5 times | | Parameter or structure failure | 2 times (a deterministic error will not improve by waiting, so after two it gives a hint to change course) | | Retryable failure / the same tool failing repeatedly | 5 times | | Successes without progress | 4 times | A fingerprint keeps at most 240 characters of detail. Circuit breaking looks at how many times the same problem repeats, not at how many calls were made in total, so a ten-thousand-call tool budget will not be burned away by a single infinite loop. What an error looks like from the outside Every interface error uses the same structure: it marks the failure and carries an error code, a description for the user, the corresponding HTTP status, an actionable hint, and a trace id and timestamp for tracking, with the trace id and error code also written back in the response headers. Judge by the error code, not by the message text — message text changes with language and version, whereas the mapping between error code and HTTP status is the contract. Whether to wait or to act | What you see | What the system is doing | What to do | | --- | --- | --- | | Shows compacting or queued | Normal processing | Wait | | slowclient or resumerecommended appears | The subscription was uncoupled to protect the stream | Rebuild the projection through the catch-up endpoints | | Judged "user busy" | That task thread is still executing (the session lock is held) | Queue, or yield/cancel that thread | | Stopped after the same tool failed repeatedly | Fingerprint circuit breaking has tripped | Change the parameters or the path; resubmitting is useless | | Reports an output error | The one-time recovery has been used up | Change the model configuration or rephrase | | Reports insufficient quota | The admission-stage deduction did not pass | See Quota and Token Usage | | The UI and backend state disagree | The projection is behind | Refresh or re-enter; if it still disagrees, look at the runtime state | | You need to start completely over | — | Use "reset work state" (cancels the user's sessions and tasks, clears the workspace, and returns a brand-new session) | Further reading Boundary Handling — behavior and values for each boundary case Realtime — catch-up, cursors, and backpressure Context Compression — details of over-limit compression Observability — metrics and logs Troubleshooting — steps for handling real problems Every queue is bounded, and a full queue reports busy Limits and budgets Session locks and the single writer Recovery and circuit breaking What an error looks like from the outside Whether to wait or to act Further reading

title: Observability
summary: Where to start looking when something breaks — what logs, runtime metrics and alerts, monitoring and thread traces, and performance testing each tell you, and the order to work through a failure from the error message onward.
text: Observability Where to start looking when something breaks — what logs, runtime metrics and alerts, monitoring and thread traces, and performance testing each tell you, and the order to work through a failure from the error message onward. When something goes wrong, the clues are concentrated in four places: logs record what happened, runtime metrics and alerts show how loaded the system is right now, monitoring and thread traces reconstruct what a particular thread went through, and performance testing tells you how much the system can take. The four are independent and each covers its own area, and following them in this order is the fastest way to work a problem through. Observability diagram: three-layer separation of fact layer, replay layer, and profile layer Logs Logs go to two channels at once: a colorized layer on the console and a file layer with one JSON object per line. Files roll daily, their names begin with server.jsonl, and by default they sit under ./config/data/logs/server. The default level is info, and it can be overridden with the RUSTLOG environment variable; noise from third-party libraries is quieted out of the box. Retention defaults to 0, which means files are never cleaned up automatically — the system only deletes old files by day once you set an explicit positive number of days. Long-running deployments should either set retention explicitly or rotate the log directory themselves. Note that in sandbox mode nothing is written to files, and only console output is produced. The Helm (cli) logs at warn and above by default, the standalone local bridge at info/warn, and neither writes log files. Runtime metrics and alerts The admin side exposes a runtime metrics snapshot with fixed categories: blocking pools are split by database, file, CPU, and external call, each reporting call counts, queue waits, and timeouts; bounded queues report backlog and busy rejections; long-running background tasks report their running counts and any alerts; and the scheduling loop reports whether its heartbeat has stalled. Alerts carry a threshold and a severity. For a given blocking pool, timeout-class alerts (critical) are evaluated before latency-class ones (warning), so when you see a latency warning, first confirm there is no timeout still in queueing or execution. WebSocket and channel event logs WebSocket connections produce structured logs under one target, covering seven stages: open, ready, handshake, handshakeerror, message, parseerror, and close. A connection that will not open, a rejected handshake, or a message that fails to parse can each be told apart by which stage it reached. Channel runtime logs live in an in-memory ring buffer that keeps only the most recent 300 entries; identical content is deduplicated inside a 20-second flood window, nothing is written to the database, and a process restart clears the buffer. They can be queried two ways: the user side reads a user's own channel logs (/wunder/channels/runtimelogs, with /probe for an active probe and /wunder/channels/reconnect for a reconnect), and the admin side reads all of them (/wunder/admin/channels/runtimelogs, which also supports /probe). Use a probe for active connectivity and a reconnect for long-connection failures. Anything that needs long-term auditing has to be shipped to an external log system. Monitoring and thread traces Admin-side monitoring is the entry point to governance views. Sessions are labeled by status — running, waiting, queued, finished, error, cancelling, and cancelled — and you can export a session's thread log, page through its turns, or pull a snapshot (for example, /wunder/admin/monitor/{sessionid}/thread-log/export|turns|snapshot|changes). The log pane on the right side of the Bridge debug panel is the thread trace view; following a single thread's execution record starts there. Not everything has a Bridge panel: interlink governance, long-term memory, and goals are backend-only, with no Bridge UI, so those are checked through their APIs and the logs. Three performance entry points | Entry point | What it is for | Key limits | | --- | --- | --- | | Throughput | Stressing the model's streaming capacity, as concurrency × input/output tokens | Concurrency ≤ 1024; input presets 1024…1,048,576 and output presets 1024…8192, with hard caps of 16,777,216 input and 1,048,576 output; 50 runs of history retained | | Performance sampling | A health check in a real environment, sampling commands, IO, and so on | Uses one fixed administrator sampling user; data lands in the workspace at .wunderperf; a single command times out after 5 seconds | | Thread rendering stress test | Generating a large volume of round data to test front-end rendering and projection | User rounds ≤ 2000 and model rounds ≤ 2000, total entries ≤ 6,000,000; concurrent tracking jobs ≤ 8; generation timeout capped at 1 hour | Throughput and performance sampling belong to the admin side (/wunder/admin/throughput/, /wunder/admin/performance/sample). Throughput's live viewing channel (/wunder/throughput/ws) is deliberately exempt from the admin gate and is guarded instead by a single-use ticket. The thread rendering stress test deliberately sits on the user side (POST /wunder/chat/stress-threads) so it can be called with ordinary user credentials for self-testing, but a single job's data ceiling is very high, so watch for pressure under heavy load. The three differ in target and in what they measure — network and model pressure, environment sampling, and front-end data volume — so they should not be treated as one and the same panel. How performance is scored The three forms — the Honeycomb, the Beehive, and the Hull — are each scored independently on a weighted 0–100 scale, and scores cannot be added across forms. Comparisons are always made in the same environment, through the same entry point, before and after a change; the matching baselines live in the documentation's performance-baseline section. Numbers obtained on a different machine or through a different entry point are not comparable. Troubleshooting order 1. Get the structured error. When an interface fails, it returns one error object carrying an error code, a description, the HTTP status, an actionable hint for the user, and this request's trace id and timestamp; the trace id and error code are also written back in the response headers. Note the trace id first. 2. Check monitoring. Look at a session's status and turns; when a thread seems stuck, first tell apart "waiting for a person" from "queueing or waiting on a lock". 3. Match it against the logs. Search the log files by trace id; for live-connection problems, filter on the WebSocket stages; for a channel that is not getting through, check the runtime logs and the probe result. 4. Go into the trace. In the thread trace view, check each round's model calls, tool batches, and results to find the first point of divergence. Related pages Stream Events — WebSocket event fields Bridge Panel Guide — entry points for the monitoring and debug panels Logs Runtime metrics and alerts WebSocket and channel event logs Monitoring and thread traces Three performance entry points How performance is scored Troubleshooting order Related pages

title: Workspaces and the Working Directory
summary: Each user has exactly one workspace, and tools are rooted at it: a persistent local directory in the Honeycomb, or a single per-user directory on the server in a Hull deployment.
text: Workspaces and the Working Directory Each user has exactly one workspace, and tools are rooted at it: a persistent local directory in the Honeycomb, or a single per-user directory on the server in a Hull deployment. A workspace is a file space with a clear isolation policy. Isolation has exactly one layer: per user. One layer of isolation Files of different users are fully isolated; neither side can see the other. A user has exactly one workspace; there is no second "personal files / agent files" layer. User, agent instance, and workspace map one to one: one user, one agent, one workspace. Where the workspace lives | Form | Location | How to access | | --- | --- | --- | | Honeycomb (default) | A persistent directory on your machine | Browse with your system file manager; the agent reads and writes directly | | Hull | A single per-user directory under the server data root | Upload, download, and edit through the "Working directory" area in the Honeycomb's left sidebar | Three firm rules: | Rule | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Unique | Each user has exactly one workspace at a time; no second directory is opened for another agent | | Fixed | Once assigned it is fixed; a user cannot add, delete, or replace it | | Relative paths | Paths shown in the interface and exchanged through APIs are always workspace-relative; absolute paths are never exposed | What it carries Data isolation: a user can only access their own workspace; path checks use the user root as the boundary, and out-of-bounds reads and writes are rejected; the agent's file tools are rooted at this directory and no second root is derived. File persistence: the workspace is not cleaned automatically, so the files you put in and the files the agent generates are kept long term. Keep long-lived files in the workspace and transient transfers in the temporary directory. Root of configuration: the workspace is also the root of "what the agent can see" — the skills directory, knowledge files, and global settings, which the agent reads at startup to initialize. Note that the agent's model, prompts, tools, and approval mode are bound through admin-side presets and managed on the settings page, not by hand-writing files in the workspace. How to use it Access: in the Honeycomb, use the file manager directly, or the "Working directory" area in the app's left sidebar with its file tree and toolbar. In the Honeycomb's left sidebar, below the workspace, there is a "Working directory" area with a file tree and an upload / create / refresh / multi-select toolbar. In conversation: hand files to the agent, or have it read and write files in the workspace directly. Reference into chat: pick "Reference into chat" from a file row's menu to bring the file into the input area. Download (Honeycomb): select files in the tree to download; multi-select bundles them into an archive. Organizing tips: create subdirectories by project or topic, one directory per project and split source material from output inside it; put files the agent should analyze into the workspace first, then mention the path or filename in your message; the reports and scripts the agent generates also land in the same tree, to be tidied as needed. Delete files you no longer need and give files meaningful names. Usage and space The bottom of the file area shows used capacity, file count, and directory count. Statistics use bounded traversal and are marked as a lower bound for very large directories. In a Hull deployment with a quota configured, uploads are rejected with a prompt to clean up once the limit is hit; without a quota, only used capacity is shown, with no quota denominator. The Honeycomb's local boundary The Honeycomb runs locally, and its working directory is a persistent directory on your machine rather than a temporary sandbox: Contents persist and are not periodically cleaned. Whether the agent can access local paths depends on local security settings. It is more flexible, but you should understand the directory boundaries. Common mistakes A workspace cannot be moved to another directory, nor can a second one be added. More agents do not mean more working directories: each user has one agent instance and one workspace. Files no longer split into a "personal container" and an "agent container"; that layering is gone, and the user and the agent share the same workspace. Do not write absolute paths: the API exchanges paths relative to the workspace root, and absolute paths are not exposed.
