title: Sessions and Rounds
summary: How a conversation is numbered: threads, user rounds, model rounds, timeline entries, and the authoritative counting conventions.
text: Sessions and Rounds How a conversation is numbered: threads, user rounds, model rounds, timeline entries, and the authoritative counting conventions. The numbering keeps "how many times the user asked" separate from "how many steps the agent took". Statistics, replay, queueing, and token accounting all depend on this coordinate system. Hierarchy | Concept | What it is | Decided by | | --- | --- | --- | | Thread / session | The main body of a continuous stretch of execution and dialogue; one session id runs through scheduling, locking, and state | Starting a thread starts a session; a subagent is an independent session traced back by its parent session id | | User round | One accepted human input | Incremented in the session on acceptance; a uniqueness constraint guarantees "one root per round" | | Model round | One model call of the engine's main loop, which may include a batch of tool calls | Incremented once per sample of the main loop | | Entry | The smallest renderable record on the timeline | Upserted by a stable entry id when it is written | These four layers are the coordinates: | Coordinate | Meaning | | --- | --- | | User round | Which user round it belongs to | | Model round | Which model call within that round (empty before sampling begins) | | Round id | The persistent id of that user round, used as the prefix of the entry identifier | | Target round | This round was started by the target driver rather than by a person, so a goal action that needs human authority is not started twice | Counting conventions One model round = one model call, not "one action". Tool calls belong to a batch within the same model round and are not counted as separate model rounds. One model round produces exactly one visible output item: refreshing several times within the same model round only updates that item and never appends duplicate bubbles. A tool-batch entry on the timeline is not an independent model round. Each tool call is its own entry (merging "in progress → done / failed" by call id), so the number of steps is usually larger than the number of model rounds. A continuation round does not consume a user round: a continuation that carries a root-round reference (for example, the target driver taking over) reuses the same user round and only adds model rounds within it. A user round publishes a change only when it is genuinely newly created; a replayed acceptance is an idempotent no-op that produces no new round and notifies no subscribers. Idempotency and queueing | Mechanism | Convention | | --- | --- | | Submit idempotency | The same client message id reuses the existing round, so a network retry does not create an extra round | | Serialization within a session | The session lock is isolated per session, with a 120-second timeout and a 5-second heartbeat; an abnormal exit releases it on timeout | | Queueing | The queue toggle is on by default; messages sent while running enter the queue and run in order | | Turning queueing off | A message sent while running is judged "user busy" and not queued (the hull warns at startup), so do not turn it off as a performance tweak | | Background delivery | Scheduled messages take the forced-enqueue path so they are not lost while competing for the lock with human messages | What appears on the timeline A session records only events with timeline value: | Entry type | State flow | | --- | --- | | Tool call | In progress → done / failed (merged by the same call id) | | Model call | Numbered by model round | | Visible reply | The output item of that model round | | Approval | Waiting → decided | | Subagent message | Uses the producer-supplied message id as a persistent identity, so a replay never becomes a new entry | | Queue ledger | Pending → running (upserted on the same entry); the interface skips it | Not recorded: transport deltas, heartbeats, progress, context occupancy, workspace updates, model usage, and streaming retries, together with lifecycle receipts (ended, status, model response, and so on — failure details are carried by the round's terminal state). These are visible in the stream but should not become empty timeline entries. How the interface reads it The chat page shows one user round per row (12 per page by default, up to 20), folding everything between the final reply into a "working process". The working process is collapsed by default; the first expansion fetches that user round's persistent entries on demand rather than pulling the entire history into the frontend. The entry-by-entry panorama lives in the "thread trace" view (80 per page by default, up to 100), with long bodies fetched in 8 KB chunks. The directory list reads the tail of each round (highest user round, that round's state, a recent-activity summary, and the backfill cursor), querying a page of sessions in one batch. How to use it When to start a new session: changing topic; needing to apply new agent settings, a prompt template, or long-term memory (an existing session's prompt is already frozen); or when the context has grown long and is starting to lose early detail. When to keep the current one: the same task is still unfinished, or you need to reference earlier output. Continuing does not recompute the base; it only adds rounds. How to point at "a certain step": give the coordinates "user round + model round", or the entry id directly; for tool batches give the entry sequence number only and do not call it "round N". Common mistakes "One round = one question and answer" — one user round can contain many model rounds, and each model round can carry a batch of tool calls. "Step count = round count" — they are not equal; steps (entries) are usually more. "A session and a thread are two things" — in this system they are the same: the session is the carrier of the conversation and its records, and the thread is its executing body. "Submitting again charges an extra round" — a retry with the same client message id is idempotent. "A subagent's input shows up in the parent session" — a sub-session's opening user message is hidden by default and skips automatic memory extraction, so it does not pollute your memory. "Token statistics = the provider's bill" — a session records context occupancy (trusting only the value the model reports), not a billing figure. Further reading The agent loop — how model rounds advance and terminate Streaming execution — the relationship between entries and deltas Context compression — how history is trimmed Long-term memory — memory isolated by scope Session states — events and state fields Hierarchy Counting conventions Idempotency and queueing What appears on the timeline How the interface reads it How to use it Common mistakes Further reading

title: Streaming Execution
summary: Events are persisted before they are pushed, a reconnect resumes by cursor, and the frontend consumes bounded views.
text: Streaming Execution Events are persisted before they are pushed, a reconnect resumes by cursor, and the frontend consumes bounded views. Streaming is not about making characters appear one by one: the process is visible in real time, what you see is what was persisted, and a dropped connection can reconnect. Persist first, then notify When the engine emits an event, it first writes it synchronously into the session record (one serial channel per session, a single transaction), and only after the transaction succeeds does it publish the change cursor and wake subscribers. That gives three guarantees: Commit order = change order: each session has its own channel and writes complete in short transactions; a failed commit does not publish a cursor. Idempotent and quiet: a replayed acceptance, an unchanged state, or duplicate feedback produces no change and notifies no one. Waking is only an accelerator: the in-process wake channel is not a correctness guarantee, so the server always keeps a polling fallback for resumption (starting at 250 ms and backing off exponentially to 4 seconds), and multiple instances converge through polling. So the text shown in the interface and the text read after a refresh come from the same source; there is no in-between state where the stream has something the store does not. WebSocket only | Channel | Purpose | | --- | --- | | /wunder/chat/ws | The main channel for chat sessions: submit, resume, watch, cancel, and approve | | /wunder/ws | The general request surface (submit one execution and receive it as a stream) | | /wunder/interlink/remotews | A browser watching a single session on a remote device; pure forwarding, not persisted | | /wunder/userworld/ws, /wunder/desktop/lan/ws | In-site sessions and LAN collaboration | The default Honeycomb form does not go through the local HTTP / WebSocket: an in-process native event channel (bounded at 128 items) delivers directly, and losing a subscription or closing a window does not cancel a round already accepted on the server. ⚠️ Chat has no SSE fallback. The server does provide SSE, but only for the external integration surface and model-proxy calls, not as a degradation channel for chat. Four classes of events | Class | Enters the timeline | Usage | | --- | --- | --- | | Entry events (tool call, model call, visible reply, approval, subagent message, compaction, round terminal) | Yes | Upserted by a stable entry id | | Transport deltas (assistant body tail chunk, command output delta) | No | Add characters only: the assistant body uses a tail chunk, command output uses a delta | | Status and receipts (session state, ended, error, session closed, queueing) | Partly (queueing is a persistent record) | Judge the lifecycle; not rendered as entries | | Wake and backfill (view changed, view needs refetching, snapshot needed, stream overflow, slow client, reconnect suggested) | No | The client resumes or refetches wholesale based on these | Statistics (context occupancy, token usage, round usage, model usage, quota) are only for panel refreshes and do not enter the timeline. Disconnection and backfill The client keeps a persistent cursor (a change sequence number) and sends it when reconnecting: | Situation | Server signal | What the client does | | --- | --- | --- | | Behind, but not by much | Resume sending change rows from the cursor | Apply incrementally in place | | Behind beyond the window | Stream overflow + reconnect suggested | Receive the signal first, then drop that subscription and reconnect by cursor | | The persistent window has been trimmed | Snapshot needed | Give up on resuming and pull one atomic snapshot | | The displayed view is behind | View needs refetching / view changed | Refetch the paged view rather than stitching entry by entry | The backfill interfaces come as a set: session change list, atomic snapshot, event paging, and single-entry body. Bounds are the default | Parameter | Value | | --- | --- | | Write queue per connection | 256 (full means slow client) | | Slow-client watermark | 2 (alarm / degrade once the queue is deeper) | | Resume page size | 200 | | Event read limit | 200 | | Heartbeat | 15 seconds | | Single message | 512 KiB (rejected when exceeded; 256 KiB for remote watch) | | Chat page / trace page | 12 (up to 20) / 80 (up to 100), response budget 128 KB / 192 KB | | Body chunk | 8 KB | The frontend consumes a view: a chat page holds only 12 user rounds, and everything between the final reply in each round folds into a "working process" that fetches that round's entries only when expanded. The trace is the entry-by-entry view (up to 8 subagent cards per row). How to judge Whether a round is over: look at the round's terminal state (with status, stop reason, and optional error and recovery action) rather than guessing that "it seems stopped". While waiting for approval or more information, the session is still within its lifecycle. Duplicate bubbles: most likely the client appended a new item instead of upserting by entry id. Locate the same item by "round id + model round". Missing characters: check whether the delta was treated as the only source. A delta only provides continuous display; the truth of the body is in the entry, so after reconnecting you should backfill rather than guess. Content gets longer after a refresh: that is normal. A refresh reads the persisted body, which may be more complete than the streamed tail chunk. Common mistakes Streaming and persistence are not two paths: events are persisted synchronously when emitted, and the cursor is published after the transaction. A disconnect is not an interrupted execution: execution continues on the server, and the client simply reconnects by cursor. SSE is not a fallback for chat; chat is WebSocket only. Fetching a few more times will not return the full history: views are deliberately bounded, and moving the full history is exactly what the design avoids. "Seeing text stream out" does not mean "the loop ran many rounds": text deltas and model rounds are two different granularities, and one round can contain thousands of deltas. Further reading Session states — the list of events and fields Chat WebSocket — protocol and envelope Sessions and rounds — entry and round granularity Real-time behavior — design principles System architecture — the layering of view and truth Persist first, then notify WebSocket only Four classes of events Disconnection and backfill Bounds are the default How to judge Common mistakes Further reading

title: Runtime and Online Status
summary: A conversation is not just static history: it also carries runtime state such as running, waiting for approval, or waiting for input, and that state tells you what the session is doing right now.
headings: Where it shows up in the interface
text: Runtime and Online Status A conversation is not just static history: it also carries runtime state such as running, waiting for approval, or waiting for input, and that state tells you what the session is doing right now. A conversation is more than a chat log. It also carries runtime state that tells you what the session is doing right now. Two layers of state The first layer is what the session is doing at this moment. | State | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Running | Actively working | | Waiting for approval | Paused on an action that needs your go-ahead | | Waiting for your input | The agent is waiting for you to add information | | Interrupting | Being interrupted | | Idle | Nothing to do, waiting for your next message | | Not loaded | Not yet loaded into memory | The second layer is a summary snapshot the interface reads directly: whether output is still streaming, whether the session is waiting, whether it is loaded, whether it is active, and whether it has already reached a terminal state. Where it shows up in the interface Session list: the status badges come straight from runtime state — a green dot means an active session, a spinning icon means running, and a waiting icon means waiting for approval or input. Session detail: the status indicator tells you which stage you are at, whether you can send a new message, and whether any approval is pending. Judging a stuck session Runtime state is the starting point for troubleshooting. | You want to know | Look at | | --- | --- | | Whether it is still running | Whether output is still streaming | | Whether it is waiting | Whether it is in a waiting state | | Whether it has finished | Whether it has reached a terminal state | | Whether it can still be observed | Whether it is loaded and active | Do not rely on a single coarse running / not-running flag. It cannot tell "still streaming" apart from "waiting for approval", and it says nothing about whether the session is loaded or has reached a terminal state. Read the full set of snapshot fields instead. When state looks inconsistent If the interface and the actual state do not match: 1. Wait a few seconds to see whether it recovers on its own. 2. Refresh the page or restart the app. 3. Use "Reset working state". Common mistakes Waiting for approval is a pause, not an ending — it is still within the session lifecycle. State belongs on the list and event pages too, not only the detail page. The event stream carries the timeline while the runtime snapshot carries the present moment; they are not the same layer. Further reading Session states — what each state means in detail The agent loop — how state changes Streaming execution — how state is pushed Two layers of state Where it shows up in the interface Judging a stuck session When state looks inconsistent Common mistakes Further reading

title: Prompts and Skills
summary: The system prompt shapes the agent's persona, and skills are its operating manuals for a class of task.
headings: A rule that is easy to trip over
Prompts, skills, and memory each cover their own ground
text: Prompts and Skills The system prompt shapes the agent's persona, and skills are its operating manuals for a class of task. An agent's behavior is decided by two things: its system prompt (who it is, how it thinks, what principles it holds) and its skills (the concrete method it follows for a class of task). The system prompt The system prompt is the agent's working manual. It sets out the role it plays, the engineering principles it follows, how it uses tools, how it calls on skills, and what memory context it remembers. The system prompt is fixed when the session is created and stays frozen afterward. This keeps the agent's behavior consistent within the same session. Skills A skill is an operating manual for the agent. It bundles a full method, execution scripts, examples and resources, and the constraints and boundaries that apply. When it needs to, the agent reads the complete skill document. A skill packages a method for a class of task, so similar tasks follow the same method and results stay consistent. Skills come in three layers. | Layer | Description | Editable | | --- | --- | --- | | Built-in | Shipped with the system | Read-only | | Custom | Created by a user or administrator | Editable | | External | Imported from outside | Depends on the source | Prompt template packs wunder supports several prompt template packs: a Chinese pack (Chinese style by default), an English pack (English style by default), and custom packs tailored as needed. To switch, open the agent settings, find "Prompt template", pick one, and save. When it takes effect: a new conversation uses the new template while existing conversations are unchanged. Changing a template and seeing no change in the current conversation is expected; starting a new conversation picks it up. To build a custom template, copy a built-in one, edit the sections (role, principles, additional notes, and so on), and save it to use. A rule that is easy to trip over Resource paths inside a skill document are written as placeholders rather than hard-coded paths. A skill lives in a different actual location in each runtime form, so the system substitutes the correct path when the skill is used. Prompts, skills, and memory each cover their own ground | | Responsibility | | --- | --- | | Prompt | Defines the long-lived, stable boundary of behavior | | Skill | Defines the additional execution protocol for a class of task | | Memory | Defines the long-term facts injected when a session initializes | The three work together, but their responsibilities are not mixed. Working with templates and skills A template has a clear role, concise principles (keep the important constraints rather than piling them on), no internal contradictions, and is tuned against real results. Skills are managed on the "Tools" page: see installed skills, enable or disable them, create a skill for a particular working scenario, and share one with the team. Combining prompt templates, skills, and models produces agents of different styles: a coding assistant, a copywriter, a data analyst, a translation expert. Common mistakes Changing a template does not affect the current conversation right away; it only affects new conversations. A skill is not just a documentation file; it is a runtime resource the agent can actively read. Memory does not rewrite the prompt every round; it is injected once at initialization. Further reading Prompts and personalization — how to work with templates Memory (core) — the design principles of memory Tool system — how tools and skills relate The system prompt Skills Prompt template packs A rule that is easy to trip over Prompts, skills, and memory each cover their own ground Working with templates and skills Common mistakes Further reading

title: Long-term Memory
summary: How the agent "remembers" your preferences, background, and long-term material—structured memory is injected once when a conversation starts, then supplemented by recall as it runs.
headings: Memory and the knowledge base are not the same
text: Long-term Memory How the agent "remembers" your preferences, background, and long-term material—structured memory is injected once when a conversation starts, then supplemented by recall as it runs. wunder's memory holds to one principle: stability over flexibility. Three core rules 1. Injected once when the session is created: long-term memory is written into the system prompt once, when the conversation starts. 2. Frozen while running: later turns do not change the system prompt. 3. Supplemented by recall when needed: while running, recall adds material, but it does not rewrite the foundation. The reason it is not updated every round: if the system prompt were rewritten each round, the agent's behavior would be unstable (drifting as the conversation goes on), cache hits would fall (making it slower), and problems would be hard to trace (you could not say what background it was working from at the time). One injection plus freezing equals stable behavior plus a traceable background. What memory looks like Memory is made of structured fragments, not one long free-form passage. A fragment is found by lookup, replaced without affecting the rest, marked invalid when outdated, and carries traceable version relationships. What memory can hold Who you are: preferences and habits, work background, past decisions. Organizational knowledge: team rules and standards, project background, domain expertise. Personalization: adjusting the answer style to your preferences, referring to your past context, and giving targeted suggestions. Initialization injection vs runtime recall | | Initialization injection | Runtime recall | | --- | --- | --- | | Timing | When the session is created | During the conversation | | How | Written into the system prompt | Added as a tool result | | Effect | Becomes the session's cognitive foundation | Does not rewrite the foundation | | Scope | The life of the whole session | The current round | Managing memory View: see the current memory in the agent settings. Add: tell the agent "remember this preference," or add it by hand in settings. Delete: remove fragments that are outdated or unneeded. Update: add a new fragment to replace an old one. When it takes effect: a new conversation uses the latest memory at once; an existing conversation is unaffected and keeps using the memory from when it was created. So after updating memory, you need to start a new conversation for it to apply. Memory and the knowledge base are not the same | | Memory | Knowledge base | | --- | --- | --- | | Content | Structured personal / organizational facts | Documents, material, and standards | | When used | Injected at initialization | Retrieved while running | | Update frequency | Relatively stable | Can be updated often | | Good for | Preferences, background, decision records | Reference material, technical documents | Easy things to get wrong Memory is not updated every round; it is injected once at initialization. The results of recall are not written back into the system prompt; they are only a temporary supplement. More memory is not better: too much crowds the context and can interfere with judgment. Further reading Memory (core) — the design principles of memory Prompts and Skills — how the system prompt is organized Workspaces and Working Directory — workspace management Three core rules What memory looks like What memory can hold Initialization injection vs runtime recall Managing memory Memory and the knowledge base are not the same Easy things to get wrong Further reading

title: Quota and Token Usage
summary: Each model request costs 1 credit and 1000 are granted daily; token usage is observed only and never deducted.
text: Quota and Token Usage Each model request costs 1 credit and 1000 are granted daily; token usage is observed only and never deducted. Quota limits how many model requests you can make. Regular users receive 1000 credits per day, the same regardless of organization or level. Unused credits accumulate. The grant is applied once on the day's first use or account adjustment; days when nothing was used are not backfilled. Each real model request costs 1 credit, including the next model call inside a tool loop, compaction summaries, and failed retries. Streaming chunks, standalone tool execution, and history replay cost no credits. A request consumes a credit even if it fails; when the balance is insufficient, no new model request is dispatched. Administrators and unregistered virtual users are not limited by quota. Viewing and adjusting On the user side, "My Profile" shows the current balance and the daily grant. Administrators can set the balance directly in "User management → Settings", or grant and deduct credits: A value set directly is the final balance after the day's grant is carried over. A grant increases "cumulative granted", while a deduction counts toward "cumulative used"; an operation is rejected when the balance is insufficient. The account shows several numbers: available credits, cumulative granted, cumulative used and administrative deductions, the daily grant, and the most recent grant date. Multiple sessions share one user credit account, and concurrent requests cannot overdraw it. User levels still accumulate experience but no longer award credits. On the first upgrade, an old token-balance account is initialized to 1000 credits and is not converted from its historical token count; a restart afterward does not reset the balance either. Tokens are for observation only Token usage continues to describe a model's input, output, reasoning, and context size, and it never affects the credit deduction. A short request and a long request both cost 1 credit. The token metrics you can see include: Context occupancy: the context size most recently observed. The cumulative model tokens consumed within one user request. Model usage events, plus the request count, whether it was charged, the credit consumed in that turn, and the account snapshot for each real model request. In a session, "model request count" and "credit consumption" are two different metrics: for a regular user, one billable model request normally increases each by one; in an exempt case such as an administrator, the request count still increases but credit consumption stays at zero. The account snapshot only shows the balance at that moment and does not represent how much this request deducted. Old credit records are kept only for reading history. title: Goal Mode
summary: Goal mode is a session-level persistent goal driven by a model-round budget — set it once, and the agent keeps going on its own until it completes, gets blocked, or spends the budget.
headings: Boundaries that are easy to misread
How the model operates on a goal
A few points that are often misread
text: Goal Mode Goal mode is a session-level persistent goal driven by a model-round budget — set it once, and the agent keeps going on its own until it completes, gets blocked, or spends the budget. ## What it is Goal mode hangs a goal on a session and pairs it with a driver that lives only in the current process. Whenever the session goes idle, the driver submits the next continuation (a goal round), and each round spends one unit of the model-round budget; whether it keeps going or stops is decided by the budget, the phase, and whether the goal is blocked. A goal carries this information. | Item | Meaning | | --- | --- | | Objective | What to do, up to 4,000 characters | | Phase | One of active, paused, blocked, complete — these four and nothing else | | Continuation-round budget (maxgoalrounds) | The most automatic continuations that may run; defaults to 256 when the goal is created | | Started rounds (roundsstarted) | Only ever increases; it is never reset backwards | | Revision | Increments on every change; an update must carry the goal id and its exact current revision, and a mismatch is rejected (compare-and-set on revision) | | Blocked reason | When blocked, a machine code (blockedcode) plus a plain-language explanation (blockedmessage) | When to use it | Situation | Recommendation | | --- | --- | | Long tasks with a clear completion condition that the model should push forward over several rounds | Use goal mode | | Something a single round of Q&A can resolve | Just send a message | | Work that needs you in the decision loop often | Talk directly, and add the question panel when needed | | You only want the current round to go deeper | An ordinary round is enough; a model round has no built-in one-step-one-answer limit | The four phases | Phase | Meaning | How it is entered | How it is left | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | active | Able to continue | Create a goal, or resume | paused / blocked / complete | | paused | Sitting still; a person can resume at any time | A manual pause, or a continuation round that was interrupted | Resume | | blocked | Automatic continuation stops | The model self-reports the same blocking condition once at least 3 consecutive continuation rounds have run; or the driver fails to enqueue (queue-failed) | Resume (after the blocking condition is resolved) | | complete | Achieved | The model or a person marks it complete, and only when it is truly done | Reopen with a new goal | Whether the next round starts depends on a single gate: the phase is active, the goal is armed inside the process, and roundsstarted has not reached the budget — all three must hold to continue. A person's message always wins; a continuation round never competes with a person for the session. Boundaries that are easy to misread The budget is counted in model rounds, not tokens. The system does not track how many tokens a goal burns, there is no token budget, and there is no design in which the budget runs out and drops the goal into some restricted state. There is no cooldown between rounds. As soon as the session is idle, the driver immediately decides whether to send the next round. "Blocked" does not mean "hard": difficulty, uncertainty, and unfinished work are not reasons to report blocked. The agent must name a concrete blocking condition that persists across rounds. Arming is not persisted Whether a goal is armed is an in-process flag and is not stored in the database. After a process restart, a session restore, or a fork, the driver will not pick up automatically even if the phase is still active — it has to be armed again with an explicit updategoal carrying action=resume. When asking why a goal stopped moving, first check whether it is still armed. How the model operates on a goal The model side operates on a goal through three built-in tools. | Tool | Effect | | --- | --- | | getgoal | Reads the current goal, including the id and revision that updategoal requires; the authoritative value must be fetched before an update | | creategoal | Infers and creates a goal from a person's direct request; the objective is required and the round budget is optional | | updategoal | Edit / pause / resume / complete / report blocked (action=blocked); needs the goal id plus the current revision, and reporting blocked is rejected before the minimum round count is reached | Authority does not come from anything the model writes: human entry points stamp source = "human" onto the turn and the goal-round driver stamps goalround. Edit, pause, and resume are allowed only in a person's round; complete and report-blocked are additionally allowed in the goal's own automatic continuation rounds. The Honeycomb (desktop) does not expose these three tools for users to pick (they are hidden built-in capabilities); the runtime injects them per session, and the Beehive (web) and the Helm (cli) reuse the same injection. Where it is available | Entry | Location | | --- | --- | | API | GET/PUT/DELETE /wunder/chat/sessions/{id}/goal (user side; requires an ownership check) | | Slash command | /goal [ \|clear\|edit \|pause\|resume] | | Beehive | A goal bar in the message area | | Honeycomb | A goal banner above the input box, with inline editing | | Helm | The /goal command | | Bridge | No goal UI (the governance surface offers no goal operations) | A few points that are often misread A goal does not stop on a token limit; it looks only at the round budget, the phase, and arming. After a service restart an active goal does not resume on its own; a resume action is needed to arm it again. The model cannot mark a goal blocked at will: the same blocking condition must persist across at least 3 continuation rounds. A goal is not "a tool named goal" but three tools — getgoal, creategoal, updategoal; the old single tool and the old injection marker no longer exist. The Bridge has no goal panel; use the Beehive, the Honeycomb, or the Helm. Clearing a goal does not undo work already done: messages, tool results, and file changes already stored are kept. title: Companion System
summary: A companion is a visual layer attached to an agent — a ZIP companion package plus a sprite sheet that follows the runtime state and takes no part in any execution logic.
headings: What a companion package looks like
text: Companion System A companion is a visual layer attached to an agent — a ZIP companion package plus a sprite sheet that follows the runtime state and takes no part in any execution logic. A companion is a visual layer of company: it plays an animation that matches the session's runtime state and occasionally shows a message bubble. It takes no part in execution and does not affect scheduling; deleting a companion changes no functionality. What a companion package looks like A companion package is a ZIP that holds exactly two things: a manifest and a sprite-sheet image. The manifest (pet.json) is JSON and states the companion's id, display name, and description, along with where the sprite-sheet file lives. The sprite sheet is a single image whose path the manifest gives. Size limits: the whole ZIP is at most 24 MB, and the single sprite-sheet file is at most 18 MB. Import guards against path traversal inside the archive. Companion files live in one fixed companion directory (config/data/companions/global, overridable through WUNDERCOMPANIONSROOT); embedded forms such as the Honeycomb and the Helm pin this directory to their own data directory. The directory starts empty, so no companion package ships built in and an empty list is normal. Sprite-sheet specification Every frame is a fixed 192 × 208 pixels, and frames of the same state line up horizontally in the same row; one state occupies one row. The row number is the state (rows 0–8): | Row | State | Row | State | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 0 | idle | 5 | failed | | 1 | running-right | 6 | waiting | | 2 | running-left | 7 | running | | 3 | waving | 8 | review | | 4 | jumping | | | The session's runtime state maps to an animation row: running → running (row 7), completed → jumping (row 4), waiting → waiting (row 6), error → failed (row 5), and everything else falls back to idle (row 0). Clicking the companion plays the waving animation once. A companion package may declare fewer rows or frames: out-of-range rows or frames are degraded by a bounds check and never crash. How each form presents it | Form | Presentation | | --- | --- | | Honeycomb (Windows) | Native floating window: a Win32 layered window per pet, with dragging and the frame clock on a separate message thread that does not occupy the UI thread | | Honeycomb (Linux) | No equivalent floating window; the desktop pet exists only on Windows | | Beehive | An in-page overlay that follows the chat state | | Bridge | A companion management panel: upload, edit, delete, and export global companions | | Helm | No companion UI; it only points the companion directory at the local data directory | Scale and position | Item | Range | | --- | --- | | Stored / menu scale | 0.5–1.6 (presets 0.5 / 0.8 / 1.0 / 1.2 / 1.4 / 1.6) | | Render scale | 0.5–1.8 | | Position | Clamped to the screen work area with margins kept; drag results are saved | The Honeycomb stores position, per-companion show / scale overrides, and the global message-hint switch in a local file; the Beehive stores them in the browser (clearing browser data resets position and preferences). Who can change companions The user side is read-only: four GET endpoints only — the global list, one companion's detail, its sprite sheet, and its exported package (/wunder/companions/global). All adding, changing, and deleting sits on the administrator side (/wunder/admin/companions): list, import, edit and delete, sprite sheet, export package. The import request-body limit matches the ZIP limit (24 MB). A "private companion" in the Beehive takes effect only in the current browser and is not uploaded to the server; a global companion is uploaded by an administrator through the Bridge and is then visible to all users. The Bridge is the only upload path. Easy to get wrong A companion is not "another kind of agent"; it is only the visual shell of an agent, and one agent binds one companion. Users cannot upload a companion to the server from the Beehive; server-side companions are always managed by administrators through the Bridge, and private imports stay in the local browser. The Honeycomb on Linux has no desktop floating window — the overlay is a Win32 implementation with no Linux equivalent. Companion animation does not affect task execution: the runtime state drives the animation, not the other way around. The system ships no companion package; an administrator uploads them. title: Boundary Handling
summary: Context overflow, network interruption, tool failure, queued tasks — the system stays stable under these boundary conditions instead of crashing outright.
headings: A dropped connection: automatic reconnect plus event replay
Oversized tool output: three layers of containment
Several requests at once: queueing plus priority
text: Boundary Handling Context overflow, network interruption, tool failure, queued tasks — the system stays stable under these boundary conditions instead of crashing outright. Conversations grow longer, the network jitters, tools error out, and several requests arrive at once; under these conditions wunder aims to hold steady rather than collapse as a whole. The three handling principles Contain the blast radius: when one link fails, it does not drag the others down with it. Stay recoverable: failure is not the end; the system keeps a recovery path. Stay reviewable: problems of the same kind can be categorized, reproduced, and verified. Context overflow: graduated compression As a conversation grows longer and tool results pile up, the total token count can exceed the model's ceiling. The system compresses progressively in four levels: | Level | What it does | Loss | | --- | --- | --- | | Level 1 | Remove intermediate tool results | Very low | | Level 2 | Summarize the conversation history | Medium | | Level 3 | Remove earlier parts of the conversation | Higher | | Level 4 | Emergency degradation | Very high | The system prompt never takes part in compression and stays frozen, so compression never changes the agent's behavioral setup. A dropped connection: automatic reconnect plus event replay A connection can drop because of network jitter. After a disconnect the interface shows a prompt first, then reconnects automatically with exponential backoff (1 s → 2 s → 4 s → 8 s → 16 s, up to 32 s). Events that were not pushed during the disconnect are cached and replayed once the reconnect succeeds; if the replay also fails, the interface prompts for a manual refresh. Tool failure: handled by type | Failure type | Handling | | --- | --- | | Wrong parameters | The agent corrects the parameters itself and retries | | Permission denied | Execution stops and waits for your approval | | Temporary error (file locked, network jitter) | Automatic retry | | System error | Limited retry plus degradation | Oversized tool output: three layers of containment | Layer | Role | | --- | --- | | Execution budget | Caps the size of a single output | | Result trimming | Keeps the head and tail when the limit is exceeded | | Pre-model check | Trims once more before the input reaches the model | A trimmed result tells the agent explicitly that it was cut, so the agent can switch strategy. Several requests at once: queueing plus priority When a conversation is busy, new requests are not turned away but queued and run in turn once it is free. Priority runs from high to low: administrators > high priority > normal > low priority. What you can do Long conversations: watch context usage and compress proactively with /compact when needed; start a new session once a topic is done. Network jitter: when the interface shows "connection lost", wait for it to reconnect automatically instead of refreshing repeatedly; if the reconnect fails, refresh manually as prompted. Tool failure: read the failure notice to find the cause and adjust as it suggests (for example, give the correct file path); if it keeps failing, ask an administrator to check the system logs. System exceptions: if there is no response for a long time, try cancelling or resetting first; if the state is clearly wrong, use "reset working state"; if it keeps happening, ask an administrator to troubleshoot. Easy to get wrong An agent answering does not mean everything is fine; look at whether it stays stable over time and whether it catches failures when they happen. Retrying is not a cure-all; different error types take different handling. Boundary cases are not rare; they show up often in long conversations and complex tasks.
